Feature: BS-12 — autonomous governed Web investigation CLI MVP
### Summary

Implement BeeAgent BS-12 as the complete operator-facing autonomous Web reconnaissance and information-disclosure workflow using BeeScan It13, existing governed HTTP execution, AI profiles, authenticated evidence and persistent Investigation Cases.

### Type

- [x] Feature
- [ ] Fix
- [ ] Docs
- [ ] Chore
- [ ] Idea

### Roadmap / iteration

- Iteration: BS-12 — Autonomous Web Investigation CLI MVP
- Stage: 8 — AI-Guided Authorized Web Investigation
- Goal from `docs/product/beescan_roadmap.md`: Enable bounded autonomous Web research through one Target + Task CLI entrypoint, without fixed-family rejection or separate execution infrastructure.
- Dependency: BeeScan It13, separately approved Issue.

### Context

The real PortSwigger backup-file disclosure task failed with `unsupported_investigation_task`, zero HTTP requests, one AI call and exit code 5.

Current `adaptive_objective()` accepts only fixed disclosure objectives. `run_adaptive()` constructs its available capabilities exclusively from two BeeScan families. Existing `execute_investigation()` defaults to `adaptive=False`.

The current persistent Case schema is limited to two family outcomes and cannot directly represent generalized discovery.

BeeAgent already owns managed egress, governed capture, source authentication, approval policy, local operator context, sensitive output and ArtifactAPI. These mechanisms must be reused, not replaced.

### Scope

**Included**

- Make the general evidence-driven investigation the normal CLI behavior when the approved BeeScan investigation functionality is enabled.
- Preserve `./start.sh beescan investigate --target URL --task TEXT`, existing trusted-local authorization, file-based input where supported, `--inspect`, `--resume` and compatible legacy behavior.
- Keep `--adaptive` accepted for compatibility without making it mandatory.
- Remove fixed-family AI classification as a prerequisite for safe general discovery.
- Start permitted discovery from the approved target origin using existing governed HTTP/HTTPS execution.
- Reuse current managed egress, DNS/IP pinning, TLS checks, destination restrictions, scope reauthorization, process isolation and actual request accounting.
- Implement bounded same-origin GET scheduling from BeeScan-supported discovery candidates, including standard discovery resources and evidence-observed or tightly derived references.
- Add deterministic queue ordering, canonicalization, duplicate suppression and validated per-action identity.
- Enforce explicit request, step, depth, response-size and deadline ceilings through validated BeeAgent configuration.
- Preserve current configuration source of truth. Extend bounds only where the existing two-step/six-request limits block meaningful general investigation.
- Apply current authorization and destination checks to every actual request without requiring additional manual confirmation for normal in-scope GET operations.
- Reuse existing named AI profiles for objective interpretation, hypothesis assistance and bounded explanation where deterministic analysis is insufficient.
- Supply only sanitized, redacted, bounded context to AI. Model outputs must never directly authorize URLs, methods, payloads, hosts, filesystem access or shell commands.
- Invoke BeeScan It13 after authenticated observations to select and reevaluate supported actions.
- Reuse existing specialized framework-version and debug-disclosure capabilities when supported by evidence.
- Analyze discovered textual source/configuration material through the BeeScan domain API and existing protected transient-content boundary.
- Present exact requested sensitive values only through the approved trusted-local terminal mechanism after authenticated evidence validation and successful publication checks.
- Extend persistent Case state and checkpoints for discovery actions, hypotheses, decisions, evidence references, actual metrics and continuation.
- Preserve safe inspection of legacy Case schema v1 and provide explicit versioned handling for new general-investigation checkpoints.
- Prevent incomplete, altered, foreign, stale or corrupted checkpoints from establishing a completed action, trusted secret or finding.
- Implement fresh-process `--inspect` and `--resume`, avoiding unnecessary repetition of sufficiently authenticated completed work.
- Produce terminal output, structured JSON and Markdown reports showing the task, inspected resources, observations, supported answer or CANDIDATE, hypotheses, limitations and evidence-informed next actions.
- Report exact request counts, AI-call counts and elapsed duration; include real token/cost usage only when provided by the configured transport.
- Preserve truthful distinctions between successful investigation, incomplete/partial research, refusal, timeout, no disclosure and execution error.
- Update relevant CLI, configuration, investigation, Case, artifact and operator documentation.

**Excluded**

- A second BeeAgent or BeeScan runtime, scheduler, database, generic crawler or multi-agent system.
- Playwright, browser automation, proxy infrastructure or generic shell execution without a demonstrated MVP blocker.
- Unbounded wordlists, broad scanning, out-of-scope requests, arbitrary AI-generated URLs or unsafe HTTP methods.
- Autonomous exploitation, credential attacks, authentication bypass or destructive actions.
- Automatic Bug Bounty submissions or human VERIFIED findings.
- New BeeSDK/BeeUI interfaces or Web UI implementation.
- Hardcoded laboratory paths, expected responses, credentials or solutions.
- Unrelated refactoring, new services and unnecessary dependencies.

### Deliverable

One working operator command:

`./start.sh beescan investigate --target URL --task "Natural-language information-disclosure objective"`

Execution:

`Governed Discovery → BeeScan Hypothesis/Decision → Governed Action → Authenticated Evidence → Replan / Stop → Answer or Useful PARTIAL`.

Outputs include terminal summary, safe JSON/Markdown reports, investigation Case, evidence references, metrics and resume context.

### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] The normal Target + Task CLI invocation uses the general investigation workflow without requiring `--adaptive`.
- [ ] An unfamiliar but safely researchable objective reaches at least one governed HTTP discovery action instead of failing solely because its category is absent from an enum.
- [ ] Actual authenticated HTML/resource observations reach BeeScan It13 and change the next supported action.
- [ ] The runtime follows a bounded chain of resources without code changes for new file names, paths or site structures.
- [ ] Candidate URLs and AI proposals pass existing host authorization, destination, method and request-budget checks before network execution.
- [ ] One previously unsupported authorized information-disclosure scenario is resolved end-to-end using actual HTTP evidence and no hardcoded challenge logic.
- [ ] A separate unfamiliar scenario demonstrates portability of the same implementation.
- [ ] A patched/non-disclosing target produces no fabricated credentials, CANDIDATE or VERIFIED finding.
- [ ] An unresolved or capability-limited task returns a useful PARTIAL/INCONCLUSIVE report with actual observations, attempted hypotheses, gaps and recommended next actions.
- [ ] No extra per-request operator confirmation is required for permitted in-scope GET actions.
- [ ] Request, step, depth, response-size and time ceilings are enforced with accurate metrics.
- [ ] Sensitive source content and requested secrets are absent from AI input, logs, ordinary artifacts, Case checkpoints and non-TTY output.
- [ ] Fresh-process inspection and resume validate identities and provenance and avoid unnecessary repeat execution.
- [ ] Corrupted checkpoints, changed DNS/IP, denied authority, cross-origin redirects and unsupported proposed actions fail closed.
- [ ] Existing framework-version, debug-secret, fixed investigation, assessment and prior Case workflows remain compatible.
- [ ] Real configured AI and real governed HTTP/HTTPS paths are exercised before PR.
- [ ] The shared BeeScan It13/BS-12 product Definition of Done passes.

### Change level

- [ ] low-risk
- [ ] runtime-risk
- [x] security-sensitive

Reason: External HTTP execution, task-driven action selection, AI input, destination policy, persistent security evidence and sensitive-value presentation are affected.

### Config / Contract impact

- [ ] no config or contract change expected
- [x] `config/settings.yml` may change
- [x] new required keys must be validated fail-fast
- [ ] module contract may change
- [x] artifact contract may change
- [x] capability / integration contract may change
- [x] CLI/runtime/transport behavior may change
- [x] docs update likely required

Source of truth:

- `config/settings.yml`
- `src/beeagent_module/integrations/beescan/investigation.py`
- `src/beeagent_module/integrations/beescan/probe.py`
- `src/beeagent_module/integrations/beescan/case_state.py`
- `src/beeagent_module/integrations/beescan/local_cli.py`
- Existing capture, egress, HTTP, source-verification, policy and ArtifactAPI implementations.
- BeeScan It13 public domain decision contracts.

Configuration rules:

- Reuse the current `beescan.investigation.adaptive` configuration instead of creating a second planner configuration.
- Validate any new limits explicitly with bounded ranges and fail-fast behavior.
- Keep authorization, active provider selection and security policy host-owned.
- Preserve previous Case schema interpretation; use explicit versioned handling for new checkpoint structure.
- Do not bypass existing immutable Git dependency checks in production.

### Tests

**Automated**

- [x] unit/integration tests
- [x] `pytest -q`

**Smoke / runtime**

- [x] smoke checks through expected entrypoint
- [x] log verification
- [x] artifact verification

**Quality / security**

- [x] SAST
- [ ] SCA
- [x] DAST
- [ ] IAST
- [x] fuzzing
- [x] some checks are not applicable

Required verification:

1. Real operator CLI using an unfamiliar natural-language objective and governed HTTP discovery.
2. PortSwigger backup-file disclosure laboratory or a newly launched equivalent, without source-code challenge hints.
3. Distinct unfamiliar disclosure fixture or authorized target with different resources and naming.
4. Patched/non-disclosing target and negative/misleading response fixtures.
5. One unsupported-by-capabilities task producing an evidence-backed useful partial result.
6. Regression of existing framework-version and diagnostic-secret workflows.
7. Actual AI profile invocation with strict structured result and sanitized context checks.
8. Evidence-dependent action changes and multi-step discovery with actual request accounting.
9. Fresh-process Case inspect/resume, interrupted actions, corrupted checkpoints, altered source identity and replay protection.
10. Denied destination, changed DNS/IP, redirect, TLS, scope and deadline boundaries.
11. Prompt injection, unsafe URL proposals, unsupported HTTP methods, malicious response bodies and oversized/malformed content.
12. TTY and redirected-output secret handling; logs, JSON, Markdown and checkpoint redaction.
13. Safe egress lifecycle and verified source/artifact read-back.
14. Full frozen BeeAgent tests, affected BeeScan tests, package build, `git diff --check`, applicable static/type/SAST checks, bounded DAST-style route misuse and parser fuzzing.
15. Independent verification, final BeeMCP reviews and hosted CI for both repositories.

SCA is required only if an approved dependency change is introduced. IAST is not a default gate without a demonstrated need.

No mock-only or AI-only test is sufficient for product acceptance.

### Artifacts

Reuse the existing BeeAgent ArtifactAPI and run storage layout.

Expected safe outputs include the existing investigation status and Case reports, with compatible extensions for:

- inspected resources and discovery steps;
- normalized evidence references;
- hypotheses and decisions;
- action completion and stop reasons;
- redacted answer/CANDIDATE metadata;
- useful partial-report guidance;
- exact request, AI-call and elapsed-time metrics;
- token/cost status when available.

Persisted state must not contain raw secret values, unrestricted response bodies or unsafe model traces.

Existing Case v1 artifacts remain inspectable.

### Security notes

- External connector involved: existing AI profile and governed HTTP/HTTPS execution only.
- Email / attachment input involved: no.
- File/path handling involved: yes; URLs, resource references, checkpoint reads and artifact writes.
- Dependency changes involved: none expected.
- Serialization/parsing involved: yes; untrusted HTTP content, AI output and persistent Case state.
- Module / capability boundary involved: yes; BeeScan proposes, BeeAgent authorizes and executes.
- Approval and target scope must remain enforced at the actual network boundary.
- AI claims cannot establish vulnerability facts, trusted source identities or execution permission.
- Sensitive exact-value presentation is restricted to the existing trusted-local protected output boundary.
- Human verification and Bug Bounty submission remain separate explicit actions.

### Definition of Done

- [ ] Target + Task works through the normal CLI without a required adaptive flag.
- [ ] Real authenticated discovery and evidence-driven multi-step research work end-to-end.
- [ ] At least one previously unsupported authorized disclosure scenario is solved without hardcoded challenge behavior.
- [ ] A distinct unfamiliar scenario demonstrates portability.
- [ ] Patched and unsolved targets return truthful, useful outcomes.
- [ ] All existing authorization, DNS/TLS, managed-egress and request-budget boundaries remain intact.
- [ ] Case state, checkpoints, inspect/resume and legacy compatibility work correctly.
- [ ] Logs, reports, artifacts, AI inputs and redirected output exclude sensitive values.
- [ ] Metrics reflect actual execution.
- [ ] Full frozen tests, package build, targeted security checks and independent verification pass.
- [ ] Relevant documentation and artifact contracts are updated.
- [ ] Coordinated BeeScan It13 acceptance and hosted CI pass before PR completion.
- [ ] No unrelated dependency, lockfile or infrastructure change is introduced.
- [ ] `version not changed`.

### Notes

- Coordinate with the BeeScan It13 Issue as one product increment, using separate repository ownership and branches.
- Use the local editable BeeScan dependency only through the existing approved local development mechanism.
- Restore the reviewed production Git dependency before final BeeAgent merge.
- Do not commit the local editable dependency override as a production configuration.
- Fix missing parsers, action semantics, reports, metrics and integration defects inside the approved BS-12 branch before PR.
- Do not introduce a separate numbered iteration for an implementation defect discovered during the shared acceptance process.
- If a laboratory cannot be fully resolved within authorized bounded capabilities, produce a truthful partial result and separately demonstrate a successful previously unsupported scenario.
- Do not modify BeeSDK, BeeUI or unrelated modules.
- Do not create commits, PRs or merge changes without explicit user approval.

title: Gmail Trigger's error handling keeps the new poll back-off from ever engaging (polls every minute through 401/429)
source_text:
Gmail Trigger's error handling keeps the new poll back-off from ever engaging (polls every minute through 401/429)
### Bug Description

With `N8N_SCHEDULER_POLL_TRIGGERS_ENABLED=true` and `N8N_POLLER_DURABLE_CURSORS_ENABLED=true`, a failing poll trigger backs off (`poll-backoff.service.js`, which already maps 429 + Retry-After and 401/403). The Gmail Trigger never reaches it, because it catches its own API errors and returns "no new mail":

```ts
// packages/nodes-base/nodes/Google/Gmail/GmailTrigger.node.ts (same on master today)
if (this.getMode() !== 'manual') {
    nodeStaticData.lastTimeChecked ??= +now;          // set before the try, on every scheduled poll
}
...
} catch (error) {
    if (this.getMode() === 'manual' || !nodeStaticData.lastTimeChecked) {
        throw error;                                   // so this only fires for manual runs
    }
    this.logger.error(`There was a problem in '${node.name}' node in workflow '${workflow.id}': '${error.description}'`, ...);
}
...
if (!allFetchedMessages.length) {
    return null;
}
```

Because `lastTimeChecked` is set before the `try`, the rethrow only fires in manual mode, so every scheduled poll's errors are hidden. `PollTriggerTaskHandler` sees a successful empty poll and calls `recordSuccess`, never `recordFailure`. There's no back-off, no failed execution and no error workflow; the only trace is one log line per poll.

I understand the swallow-and-log was probably deliberate under the old in-memory poller, so one Gmail hiccup wouldn't stop a workflow (#5397 was closed on similar grounds). Now that the scheduler handles failures properly (back-off, cursor left in place, workflow stays active), the swallow defeats the protection the back-off was built for.

Why it matters to us: a Gmail Trigger hit `429 User-rate limit exceeded` and kept polling every minute. Each refused call pushed Gmail's Retry-After further out, and the mailbox stayed blocked for about 13 hours.

### To Reproduce

1. Enable the two settings above (`N8N_SCHEDULER_ENABLED` and `N8N_USE_WORKFLOW_PUBLICATION_SERVICE` at their default true).
2. Create a `gmailOAuth2` credential with a made-up client and access token, so Google answers 401.
3. Create a workflow with only a Gmail Trigger (typeVersion 1.4, poll every minute) using that credential, then activate it.

**Observed:**
- Activation succeeds, even though the credential can't work.
- For 6 minutes, every scheduled task finished `succeeded`, and `poller_state.consecutiveErrors` stayed `0` with `backoffUntil` null.
- No executions were saved.
- The log showed `There was a problem in 'Gmail test' node in workflow '<id>': 'undefined'` once a minute (`error.description` is undefined for this error, so the line doesn't even say what failed).

**Control:** an RSS Feed Read Trigger on the same instance, pointed at a server answering `429` with `Retry-After: 180`, logged `Poll failed; backing off`, `consecutiveErrors` went 1→3, and its polls dropped from every minute to every 4 minutes.

### Expected behavior

Gmail API errors on a scheduled poll should reach the poll back-off like other poll triggers: a 429 should honour Retry-After, and a 401/403 should get the long back-off. One option: rethrow when durable poll cursors are on (or always, now that the scheduler handles failures), and keep the log-and-continue path only for the legacy poller. Also, the log line should fall back to `error.message` when `error.description` is undefined.

### Debug Info

- Gmail Trigger typeVersion 1.4, poll mode "every minute"
- `N8N_SCHEDULER_POLL_TRIGGERS_ENABLED=true`, `N8N_POLLER_DURABLE_CURSORS_ENABLED=true`; `N8N_SCHEDULER_ENABLED` and `N8N_USE_WORKFLOW_PUBLICATION_SERVICE` at default (true)
- Docker image `docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n`, Postgres 16, single main instance

source_text:
Show HN: Waymark – A workflow engine that compiles jobs instead of replaying
Hey everyone! @mozgiii and I have been working on Waymark for the better part of the last year. Waymark’s an open source durable execution library with similar functionality to Temporal or DBOS. I fell in love with durable execution a few years ago, after working at a company with a heavy pubsub architecture. In comparison to job orchestrators that force a certain task design or special syntax, many of these durable libs lets you write business logic in regular code: `asyncio.gather` to parallelize tasks, `for` loops, conditionals, and let the runtime figure out how to run them efficiently across a cluster of nodes. But most of the current solutions require a heavy broker, runtime hacks to try to ensure deterministic workflow logic, and feel like you have to learn a whole new ecosystem just to get started. A few unique design decisions in waymark: — Write jobs in normal code (right now Python but JS coming soon). Instead of running control flow as-is, which requires booting up an interpreter to replay past state, we’ll just compile your code directly. We walk your AST and map your logic to our stackless VM bytecode. We support variables, conditionals, await, sleep, helper functions, loops... basically what you’d expect in workflow logic. — Since we’re compiling a language subset, we can proactively flag errors in your workflows locally instead of when they run in production. — It only requires Postgres as the task broker. We’ve spent a lot of time tuning our design to play nicely with its strengths and limitations; our current benchmarks show around 1500 workflows/second but we still have some more optimization work to do here. — Actions plug-and-play with FastAPI’s dependency injection syntax. So if you already have an ecosystem based on typehinting/DI, it should fit like a glove. It allows for parallelization of workflows across one machine or a whole cluster. The bulk of the work per node is done by our central Rust core - which distributes workflows to properly saturate all cores. The idea is to be as batteries included as possible with the broker, webapp, and runtime. What to use it for? It works great as the runner loop controlling agents, but it also works well for basically any task that you need to kick off in the background. It’s largely replaced our way of writing api code. Most frontend actions at this point just push to a simple REST endpoint that kick off a background job. I spent an embarrassing amount of time making our  https://waymark.sh  site interactive - it’s probably the best place to learn more. We’re starting with Python support and looking for community input on what language to ship next. Would love to hear your thoughts!

I mean strictly positive from a general welfare position. Competition through innovation is not a negative externality or else the automobile would be
I mean strictly positive from a general welfare position. Competition through innovation is not a negative externality or else the automobile would be a negative externality on account of wiping out the horse-drawn carriage industry. And the camera and photography would be a negative externality because they eliminated most of the portrait drawing industry. Automation will of course harm whichever sector of the economy remains on the manual processes, but it leads to more abundance overall. Even the people who lose jobs due to automation are better off overall. If you personally consume goods and services produced by 100 different classes of professionals, and you yourself work in one of those 100 classes of professional work, and your job gets automated, you lose out in that narrow sense, but you gain from having the products and services produced by the other 99 classes of professionals, become more abundant through automation. With respect to authenticity, that's easy to prove. Take coffee for example. People are willing to pay more for coffee that was made by hand. So what do companies do? They simply have the baristas make the coffee in front of the customers. Market incentives will produce efficient ways of proving authenticity.

Reuse P01/P02 material and independent review; preserve vetted formulas. Link only **verified** SourceRating Gumroad product URLs; otherwise show honest "in preparation" state, no fake Buy CTA.
4. **SourceRating App / AVP** — **dedicated Coming Soon / Early Access Waitlist** page. Verify if "AVP" was a transcription of "App" or another project term. Do not invent launch date, active membership or real waitlist submissions. A working signup requires approved backend, privacy/consent, deduplication, security and test confirmation; otherwise an honest noninteractive coming-soon is acceptable for Preview.

Design at **320 and 390px first**, then desktop; use selected and reviewed direction for integrated implementation. Favor high-quality typography, restrained brand system, accessible controls, source provenance and realistic data. Do not use generic SaaS gradients or decoratively fabricated engineering proof.

Claude Lead owns requirements, conflict resolution, review assignments and release; AGY owns front-end design/implementation; independent reviewer owns technical, sources/rights and visual acceptance. source_text:
Docs review: accurate, short, consistent (port of skeleton #101)
The supplymars version of myvars/skeleton#101, which was done in myvars/skeleton#107 to #110.

Review every doc in the repo so each one is correct against today's code, worth reading, and in one shared format. There are two kinds of reader:
- **Technical docs:** the main reader is an AI agent working in this repo; the second is a developer. A doc earns its place by telling them something they can't easily get from the code, from Symfony's own docs or from general knowledge.
- **`Docs/UserManual/`:** the reader is a person using the app. It is judged on accuracy against the UI and on not repeating the in-app help (`templates/help/`), not on being short for an agent.

Port the skeleton's **final state** where a doc is shared (the pattern docs and the shared ADRs). supplymars's docs diverged with their own examples, so patch in place rather than copying the skeleton's files over.

### Scope
- `README.md` (root), `CLAUDE.md`
- `Docs/README.md`, `Docs/01-…` to `Docs/13-…`
- `Docs/infrastructure/playground.md`
- `Docs/patterns/**`
- `Docs/adr/**` (fix facts only; see rules below)
- `Docs/UserManual/**` (accuracy, navigation, duplication with in-app help)

Out of scope: `vendor/`, the `myvars/form-flow` package README, and the skeleton repo.

### What to check, per file
1. **Accurate.** Check every concrete claim against the code: file paths, class, method and route names, `make` targets, console commands and options, config keys, env vars, package versions and behaviour. Run read-only commands to confirm them (`make -n`, `symfony console list`, `debug:router`, `debug:config`, `ls`, `grep`). File references and line numbers are leads, not facts.
2. **Useful.** Delete anything that is:
   - generic Symfony, Doctrine, Turbo or PHP knowledge an agent already has
   - a restatement of code that is easy to read directly. This is a likely issue in `09-cli-reference.md` (899 lines; compare with `symfony console list` and each command's `--help`) and `10-code-reference.md` (602 lines).
   - history that no longer affects how to work here (ADRs excepted)

   Keep the non-obvious parts: gotchas, "why it's done this way", things that broke before, project rules that differ from framework defaults.
3. **Not duplicated.** Each fact has one home; everywhere else links to it. Most likely overlaps:
   - `CLAUDE.md` vs `Docs/`
   - `03-architecture` vs ADR 014
   - `06-operations` vs `11-runbook` vs `13-monitoring`
   - `04-sourcing-and-pricing` / `05-features` vs ADRs 001–005, 009, 010
   - `08-security` (API auth) vs `patterns/API/README.md` vs ADR 011
   - the FormFlow docs vs the package README
   - Turbo/Modals vs ADR 007
   - the UI docs vs ADR 012
   - `UserManual/*` vs `templates/help/*`
4. **Short.** Prefer tables and bullets to prose. Use one short, plain worked example rather than several. Cut throat-clearing intros and closing summaries.
5. **Consistent format, using the templates agreed in the skeleton:**
   - Guide/pattern: H1, a 1–2 line "read when", then Rules → How to → Gotchas → Related.
   - Reference: H1, purpose line, tables, Gotchas, Related.
   - Procedure/runbook: numbered steps with commands and checks, then Troubleshooting.
   - Index: one line per doc.
   - ADR: `## Status` (one line: `Accepted.` plus an optional `Amended …` / `Superseded by …`), Context, Decision, Consequences, optional Alternatives Considered, optional Related (relative links), no date line.

   `UserManual/` keeps its own shape. The audit proposes which template each doc follows.
6. **Navigable.** `Docs/README.md` is the single index: one line per doc saying when to read it, including every pattern sub-page and ADR. Today `infrastructure/playground.md` is linked only from the runbook, and `UserManual/` only from the root README.

### Rules
- ADRs are records. Don't rewrite their reasoning or decisions. Fix stale facts (paths, names). If a decision has been overtaken, mark it "Superseded by …" or "Amended …" in the Status line rather than editing it to match.
- `12-technical-review.md` is a dated snapshot (31 March 2026). Treat it like an ADR: don't update its assessment. The audit decides whether it stays as a record, is marked as dated, or goes.
- Don't change code to match a doc. If code and doc disagree and it isn't obvious which one is wrong, list it and ask. Code problems found on the way get their own issues.
- Deleting a whole doc or merging two docs needs approval in the audit (phase 1).
- Keep anchors and paths that code and config link to. Today these are:
  - `Docs/02`, `03`, `08`, `11` and `13` from `src/`, `config/`, `deptrac.yaml`, `compose*.yaml` and `tests/`
  - ADRs 013 and 014
  - `08-security.md#rate-limiting`

  List the rest in the audit with `grep -rn "Docs/" src config tests deptrac.yaml compose*.yaml`.
- Keep the house style: plain words, short sentences, no marketing tone.

### Findings from the skeleton that apply here
Each was found and fixed in the skeleton (myvars/skeleton#107 to #110) and is confirmed in supplymars at `4b606396`. They are leads for the audit, not a full list.

**Stale or wrong facts**

| Where | Doc says | Code says | Skeleton fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `08-security.md:181` | An auth error returns `"Authentication required."` | An invalid token returns `"Invalid API token."` (`ApiAuthenticationFailureHandler.php:32`) | Error table with both cases |
| `08-security.md:357` | Sessions are in Redis "in every environment" | Check `framework.yaml` `when@test`. The skeleton's tests use `session.storage.factory.mock_file` | State dev/prod vs test |
| `CLAUDE.md:175` | The app cache holds login throttling in tests | Throttling and rate-limit counts are in the `cache.rate_limiter` pool (check `cache.yaml`) | Name the pool |
| `CLAUDE.md:141`, FormFlow/README | Chainable `->template()`, `->successRoute()`, `->allowDelete(true)` | `->csrf()` exists too | Add it |
| `patterns/FormFlow/README.md:109` | FlowModel "replaces the raw `MODEL` string constant" | History | Cut |
| `patterns/FormFlow/Usage.md:340` | ConfirmFlow flashes "Invalid CSRF token." | `ActionFlow` does; ConfirmFlow delegates to it | Fix |
| `patterns/FormFlow/Usage.md:408` | Mappers "validate input shapes" | Mappers pass fields through; validation is on the form model and entity | Drop |
| `patterns/FormFlow/Overrides.md:22` | SearchFlow "always uses" `{context}/{entity}/index` | It falls back to `shared/form_flow/index.html.twig` | Fix; also add the gotcha that `forConfirm` without `->template()` lands on `missing.html.twig` |
| `patterns/Templates/README.md:109-110` | Search `sort` and `list_item` blocks "Required: Yes" | Both have empty defaults | Fix |
| `patterns/Turbo/README.md:28`, `Frames.md` | `{model}-table` advances history | Live search uses `history.replaceState`; pagination advances | State both |
| `patterns/Turbo/Frames.md:32` | `_modal.html.twig` sits inside `components/Modal.html.twig` | The reverse: `_modal` uses `<twig:Modal>` | Fix |
| `patterns/Turbo/Frames.md:162`, `Modals.md:273` | A `turbo-frame[data-loading]` CSS block | Check: in the skeleton it was Tailwind classes on `_modal.html.twig` | Cut the block |
| `patterns/Turbo/Modals.md:218` | On success, the "flash message is appended via stream" | Success returns a refresh or redirect stream; the refreshed page renders the flash. `_frame_success_stream` carries flashes only when a frame template renders (a 422 re-render) | Explain the real path, plus the "flash not showing" / "double flash" gotcha |
| `patterns/Turbo/Streams.md:74` | Refresh is the default for "create, update, filter, action" | Filter handlers return a `RedirectTarget`, so a filter is a `redirect` stream | Drop filter |
| `patterns/InlineEdit/README.md:111` | "Preloads on hover" | `data-turbo-preload` (`InlineEdit.html.twig:22`) does nothing inside a `<turbo-frame>`, and Turbo skips preloading there | Fix |
| `patterns/InlineEdit/README.md` | (missing) | `property:` checks only that property's own rules (`validatePropertyValue`). `UniqueEntity`, `Callback` and other groups don't run, so an inline edit can save what the handler path rejects. `onSave` exceptions are form-level errors, not field errors | Add both |
| `patterns/UI/Forms.md:427` | Best practice "Add validation to form models, not entities" | Contradicts `08-security.md`'s entity-constraints rule | Drop |
| `07-testing.md:362` | `LazyValue::memoize(...)` example | Check it is used; in the skeleton it wasn't | Cut if unused |
| `07-testing.md:647` | Rector "Active rule sets" list | Check it against `rector.php`; the skeleton's was incomplete and sat under the Deptrac heading | Point at `rector.php` |
| `11-runbook.md:94` | "`RUN_MIGRATIONS=true` in `docker-entrypoint.sh`" | Check: in the skeleton it is set in `compose.prod.yaml` and the entrypoint only reads it | Fix |
| ADR 012 `:163` | "two bugs were found" | Count the kit bugs in its own local-changes table (four in the skeleton) | Fix the count |
| ADR 016 `:29` | The exact tag `dunglas/frankenphp:1.13.2-php8.5.12` | Goes stale on every bump | "Pinned to an exact version in `docker/Dockerfile`" |

**Content the skeleton's reviews found was easy to lose.** If the trim removes any of these, give each a home:
- Dev mail goes to `DEV_MAIL_RECIPIENT` and lands in Mailpit.
- The Symfony CLI certificate fix (`symfony server:ca:install`).
- Every login is remembered for 7 days (`always_remember_me`).
- Queries use bound parameters, never concatenated input.
- `DATABASE_NAME` in production env files.
- Which role sees the Help button and the `?` shortcut (check `_header.html.twig`).
- Help templates extend `help/_layout.html.twig`.
- How to assert that a message was queued (`getSent()` on `messenger.transport.async`).

**ADR shape.** Several ADRs differ:
- `## Implementation Notes` is an H2 in 008 and 011. Elsewhere it is an H3 under Consequences.
- `## Related Documentation` (007–011) and `## References` (012, 013) should become `## Related`.
- Status lines don't record amendments: 006 (flows moved to `myvars/form-flow`), 008 (amended by ADR 012), and 011 (hashed tokens, which are already in its body).
- ADRs 001–016 are complete, so there is no numbering gap to explain.

**Merges the skeleton made, to propose here in the audit.** supplymars has the same files:
- `FormFlow/Usage.md` → `FormFlow/README.md`
- `Turbo/Frames.md`, `Modals.md`, `Streams.md` → `Turbo/README.md`
- `UI/Surfaces.md` + `Typography.md` → `UI/Styling.md`
- `StimulusControllers.md` as one table with a row per controller

**Skeleton findings that don't apply here**
- `IdToEntityTransformer` (myvars/skeleton#105): supplymars uses it with integer ids (`src/Note/UI/Http/Form/Type/TicketType.php` and others), so it is real code here. Check `UI/Forms.md` describes it correctly.
- Unused frontend controllers (myvars/skeleton#106): `card_link`, `bar_chart`, `autosubmit` and `dependent_field` are used in supplymars templates. Check each controller's usage before marking any unused. `FlowForm` mounts `submit-form` here too (`templates/components/FlowForm.html.twig:16`); check whether anything calls it.
- `StateBetweenRequestsTest` and Demo removal (myvars/skeleton#104): supplymars has no Demo.

### Process
**Phase 1: audit (no edits).** For each file, produce a table row with:
- file, line count
- verdict: keep / trim / merge into X / delete
- stale facts found, with evidence
- duplication found
- target size

End with a proposed list of files and the order of PRs. **Stop here for approval.**

**Phase 2: edit**, in the approved order. Split into PRs by area if one diff would be too big to review: (1) numbered guides, (2) patterns, (3) ADRs, (4) UserManual, (5) index + root README + CLAUDE.md last, since it links to the homes the others set up.

The skeleton stacked its PRs: each was based on the one before, so its diff showed only its own change. Each PR had a fresh independent review, and every review found something load-bearing that the trim had cut.

### Acceptance
- [ ] Every path, command, class, route and config key named in the docs exists. Check with a script: grep the docs for backticked paths and `make`/`symfony console` commands, then confirm each one.
- [ ] Every relative markdown link and anchor resolves.
- [ ] No fact is stated in two places; the duplicates link to the one home.
- [ ] Each doc follows the template agreed for its kind in the audit (or has a stated reason not to); every ADR follows the ADR shape.
- [ ] `Docs/README.md` lists every doc, each with a one-line "read when".
- [ ] Line counts before and after are reported per file, and each removal of non-obvious content is justified in the PR description.
- [ ] The independent review confirms nothing load-bearing was cut (gotchas, project-specific rules, the reasons behind decisions).

AI Daily Digest — 2026-11-05
# AI Daily Digest — November 5, 2026

**Top story: OpenAI published the first end-to-end account of an AI system doing offensive security at industrial scale — and the price tag.** An autonomous pipeline built on an unreleased cyber model ran against the Linux kernel's master branch in mid-October, triaged **2,308 candidate findings**, dynamically reproduced **1,724 vulnerabilities**, and produced **948 working local privilege-escalation exploits** plus 948 candidate patches, for **$1,213,430** in API credits. The same 24 hours brought Anthropic's **FlashProve** work on cryptographic proofs of inference and OpenAI's cyber model **Daybreak Red** reaching AWS GovCloud. Running against all of it: American voters rejected data centers in **40 of 41 local ballot measures** on Tuesday, and Nikkei put the five biggest US tech firms' off-balance-sheet AI obligations at **~$3.2 trillion**, roughly double six months ago. The labs are shipping security capability faster than the public is granting them permission to build the buildings.

**A note on this edition's sourcing.** This session's network policy blocked direct access to **arXiv (including export.arxiv.org), Hugging Face, TechCrunch, The Verge, Hacker News, openai.com, worldlabs.ai, trending-repos.com, theneuron.ai and aiweekly.co**. **anthropic.com and raw.githubusercontent.com were reachable and were read directly**, and GitHub's repository-search API was reachable for named repositories (star and fork counts below are from it, read today). Everything else rests on web search results and the secondary coverage they surface; where a primary source could not be checked, the entry says so. The arXiv listing section in particular could not be verified against arXiv itself.

---

## Notable Papers & Research

### OpenAI: 948 Linux kernel root exploits, built and priced
**November 4.** OpenAI published *"A thousand fewer paths to root."* An automated pipeline — **Scout** agents selecting kernel code by reachability from low-privileged users and security relevance, then **Analyst** agents working the targets — ran against the kernel master branch in **mid-October 2026** and produced **948 distinct local privilege-escalation exploits**, each dynamically reproduced, along with **948 candidate patches**. Reported end-to-end cost: **$1,213,430** in API credits. OpenAI says it has sent hundreds of reports and patches for critical vulnerabilities to Linux maintainers, with the remainder going out through its *Patch the Planet* partners; one account puts **61 fixed upstream** at announcement time. Technical detail was withheld for safety.

**Why it matters:** this is the first time a frontier lab has published both the yield and the unit economics of autonomous vulnerability research at this scale, which makes the defensive arithmetic concrete — and makes the same arithmetic available to anyone who can rent the compute. **What to discount:** the patches are *candidates generated by the pipeline*, not 948 fixes shipped to the kernel. Circulating "bounty value" figures of **$18.9M–$66.3M** are extrapolations from Pwn2Own/TyphoonPWN comparisons, not awards, and a separate ~$1.5M figure refers to a different hardened-kernel test of 21 vulnerabilities — the two should not be combined. Sources also disagree on unique vulnerabilities versus exploit count. [OpenAI](https://openai.com/index/a-thousand-fewer-paths-to-root/) · [unite.ai](https://www.unite.ai/openai-pipeline-finds-948-linux-kernel-privilege-escalation-flaws/) · [Interesting Engineering](https://interestingengineering.com/ai-robotics/openai-agents-linux-kernel-vulnerabilities-exploits)

### Anthropic: FlashProve — zkSNARK proofs that a response came from the model you were promised
**Published November 2, updated November 3** (read directly on anthropic.com today; it reached the top of Hacker News on the 5th with 179 points). Authors: **Roy Rinberg** and **Alex Allain** (Anthropic); **Alessandro Chiesa** (EPFL, StarkWare); **Miranda Christ** (MIT, RESI); **Rahul Dalal** (Anthropic STEM Fellows Program, Succinct); **Giacomo Fenzi** (EPFL); **Ben Mayer** (Anthropic Fellows Program, MIT); **Guy Weissenberg** (EPFL). From the **Frontier Red Team**.

The problem it states plainly: a user querying a model today cannot verify the response came from the model the developer claims, rather than one swapped in by a routing service for cost reasons or by an attacker tampering with the token stream — and output quality alone is not evidence. The work advances **zkSNARKs** for provable inference, chosen for their hiding and efficiency properties, through a system called **FlashProve**. **Why it matters:** the post names **verifying compliance with AI pacing requirements** as an application, which puts a cryptographic primitive directly underneath the governance debate Amodei opened in September — pacing commitments you can check rather than take on trust. The post carries its own limitations section; treat it as progress, not a deployable guarantee. [Anthropic — provable inference](https://www.anthropic.com/research/provable-inference)

### Anthropic: the first 3D structure of a prokaryotic vault particle
**November 4** (read directly on anthropic.com). Anthropic's biology research lab reports the **first 3D structure of a vault particle found in prokaryotic cells**. Vaults are large hollow protein barrels — roughly three times the mass of a ribosome — discovered in 1986 by **Leonard Rome** and **Nancy Kedersha**, present in nearly all cells in the human body, and of **still-unknown function**. Claude was used at each step: searching across sequence literature, optimizing a particle-isolation method, and mapping the structure from cryo-EM data. A **preprint has been submitted to bioRxiv** and is not yet live.

**Why it matters:** this is the second such result in two weeks (after *"How Claude designed protein binders against scorpion neurotoxins,"* October 20), and the framing is a deliberate one — an AI lab publishing wet-lab structural biology under its own name, with the model as co-investigator rather than literature search. **What to hold back on:** no peer review yet, and the preprint link is still pending, so the structure itself is unreviewed. [Anthropic — vault particles](https://www.anthropic.com/research/investigating-vault-particles-with-claude)

### "Sparks of Weight-Space Programming" — an LLM editing another model's weights directly
**Posted November 3**, by **Rikiya Takehi** and co-authors (MIT-affiliated per secondary coverage). The claim: a general-purpose LLM can read a neural network's weights and write new values into them without gradients or a training loop. Across eight experiments with **GPT-6 Astra**, the reported headline result is diagnosing repetitive reasoning loops in **Qwen3.5-0.8B** and changing **0.016% of its weights** to lift **MATH-500 from 7.9% → 48.1%** and **GSM8K from 13.8% → 67.1%**. The authors also report Astra writing small game-playing policy networks from scratch, zero-shot.

**Why it matters:** if it generalizes, model repair becomes an inference-time edit rather than a training run — and Karpathy's "Software 2.0" framing of weights as code written by an optimizer acquires a second author. **Why to read it carefully:** the demonstrated cases are small networks and single, localized faults; a community note points out the weights were supplied as text in the prompt, with the model using code and forward passes, which weakens the word "natively." Not peer-reviewed. **[NVIDIA/auto-ontology](https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology)** — *an open library that builds a semantic context layer over enterprise metadata and serves it to any agent harness.* Apache-2.0, Python, **5,551 stars** (reported **+2,050 today**, the largest single-day gain on the board), 439 forks, 46 open issues. The README states the problem better than most: *"a revenue metric answered faster is worth nothing if the number is wrong."* Five verbs — **Discover** (generate ontologies from metadata, connect existing semantic models, build knowledge graphs), **Ground** (give agents trusted meaning for metrics and entities, reconcile inconsistent definitions across systems), **Validate** (check generated queries against certified definitions and lineage, return provenance with every answer), **Expose** (serve context via **MCP, CLI and API**), **Learn** (fold certified corrections back in). Ships a Next.js 16 frontend, FastAPI + LangChain backend, an ingestion worker, **Postgres + pgvector**, optional HashiCorp Vault, and Helm or Docker Compose deployment; NL-to-SQL is powered by **NVIDIA NIM**. **Why it's trending:** text-to-SQL agents have a correctness problem that no amount of retrieval fixes, and this is a major vendor shipping the governance layer as open source rather than a product. **What to know:** the README says the project is **currently not accepting external contributions** — open license, closed development. Benchmarking (BIRD) lives in a separate [ontology-sql-eval](https://github.com/NVIDIA/ontology-sql-eval/) repo, so the quality claims are not in this one.

**[FareedKhan-dev/kimi-k3-in-c](https://github.com/FareedKhan-dev/kimi-k3-in-c)** — *"A 2.78-trillion-parameter model. One CPU. 8 GB of RAM."* Apache-2.0, **C99**, **10,451 stars** (reported **+351 today**), 1,644 forks, 26 open issues; the engine is **176 KB** of code with **no BLAS, no framework, no GPU**. The measured table is the pitch: **8 GB RAM → 26.5 s/token**, 32 GB → 24.2 s, 64 GB → 19.8 s, **128 GB+ → 5.6 s**, against a **1.56 TB** checkpoint on disk. Below 128 GB the whole model streams off NVMe on every step; at 128 GB+ it fits in memory and the disk wait disappears. **Output is byte-identical across all four configurations — only the clock changes.** v1.0.0 reportedly cut per-token math ~**8×**, chat follow-ups **3.9×** faster, long prompts about half as costly. macOS, Windows and NEON ports, chat mode, the `ultra` preset and faster MXFP4 kernels came from outside contributors. **Why it's trending:** Moonshot's K3.1 Pro weights landing today (above) turns this from a stunt into a usable path — the same 1.56 TB download, and anyone with a laptop and patience can run it. **What to know:** 26.5 seconds per token is a demonstration of *reachability*, not a workable interactive setup, and last push was **October 2**, so the stars are riding the weights news rather than active development. The author notes in the README that they are **open to research roles and PhD positions** — the repo doubles as a portfolio.

**[zhayujie/CowAgent](https://github.com/zhayujie/CowAgent)** — *an open-source personal AI assistant and agent harness that plans tasks, runs tools and skills, and self-evolves with memory and knowledge.* MIT, Python, **47,793 stars**, **10,415 forks**, 40 open issues, created **August 2022** — one of the longest-running projects on any of these boards, now pushed into the agent-harness category. Multi-agent, multi-model, multi-channel: plug in any major LLM provider and run it 24/7 on a personal machine or server, across the web and the major IM platforms; it controls your computer and external services, creates and runs **Skills**, and builds a personal knowledge base and long-term memory. One-line install, documented at [docs.cowagent.ai](https://docs.cowagent.ai/), with English, Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese and Japanese READMEs plus Discord and WeChat communities. **Why it's here:** a four-year-old Chinese IM-bot project rebuilt as an agent harness, with a **fork-to-star ratio near 1:4.6** — far more people are running modified copies of this than of any newer repo on the board, which is a different and arguably better signal than stars. **What to know:** it controls your computer and calls external services, so the standard caution applies — scope its permissions before leaving it running unattended.

**[finic-ai/kairos](https://github.com/finic-ai/kairos)** — *open-source real-time fraud and risk decisioning, pitched as an alternative to Sardine, Sift, Riskified and SEON.* Apache-2.0, TypeScript, **213 stars**, 10 forks — tiny, but **created October 30** and already a **104-point, 31-comment Show HN**. One call on every sign-up, login, order, payment and payout returns **approve, step up, review or block** with a risk score and reasons, drawn from the subject's history, the devices/cards/addresses it shares with others, and the session; every decision is kept with the signals behind it. Workflows can ask a decision model, score, branch, call webhooks, open cases and re-decide later; human review queues turn resolutions into labels. The two differentiators it claims over the commercial incumbents: **your coding agent tunes it** (there is an **MCP server** for Claude Code and Cursor, and the README's lead image is an agent running experiments on a workflow and picking the winning variant), and **decision models catch fraud before you have labels to train on**. Ships as `@finic-ai/kairos` on npm and `finic-kairos` on PyPI, with a hosted Kairos Cloud. **Why it's here on velocity rather than volume:** this is the clearest instance yet of the pattern worth watching — a regulated, label-starved production system shipped specifically so an agent can be the one tuning it. **What to know:** six days old, 213 stars, a commercial cloud attached; no production track record, and fraud decisioning is not a domain to adopt on a Show HN.

Show HN: Datui – Explore Parquet, CSV, Arrow and S3 Data in the Terminal
Datui is a TUI application I created to make viewing large tabular datasets in Parquet, CSV, and more quick and easy (hive partitioning too). It is also a landing page for your configurable catalog of data, creates exportable charts, has built in data-quality checks, and lets you query and transform with SQL. Try it as a python module to make viewing/debugging DataFrames in a terminal session easy.  It's built on Polars LazyFrames, so only the rows on screen are read. Additionally, Datui can read custom binary formats (via a toml spec), CAN, FIX, Excel, Arrow, and others. You can install it with pip install datui, brew, winget, package managers, or a curl script. Try opening up public parquet with this:     datui s3://noaa-ghcn-pds/parquet/by_year/YEAR=2024/

[MODEL] Lane: the availability record — bitemporal, append-only, our clock (addendum 252)
## The lane

`availability-record` (docs/roadmap.json) is a bitemporal, append-only store of what was knowable about who plays, stamped by our clock. It generalises the cups' Step B store (`schema.CupLineupObservation`). The board places it **immediately below the model lanes** (252 item 7): "the NHL and NFL-QB lanes cannot declare without it — it is the first tooling that unblocks a model lane rather than waits beside one".

It is tooling, not a model. It prices nothing, it is no Desk input, and it writes no row to any existing table (item 5).

## Steps (item 7; no existing date moves)

| # | Step | Owner | Due |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The schema PR: item 1, the migration, the query command `availability`, tests 6(a)-(c), (g), (h). Filed with this Issue. | code | 2026-11-10 |
| 2 | The nflverse depth-charts feed (3(a)), its chain `availability-daily` and its 08:45 UTC timer. | code | 2026-11-12 |
| 3 | The paid feed's adapter specified, if the operator names one on 11-13 (3(c)). | architect | 2026-11-14 |
| 4 | The NHL landing feed (3(b)) and its watch, the `availability-observe` timer. | code | 2026-11-17 |
| 5 | The graph projection's candidate comparison (item 4). | code | 2026-11-20 |
| 6 | The paid feed's adapter, if one is named (3(c)). | code | 2026-11-21 |
| 7 | The graph projection's rebuild, `availability-graph-rebuild` (item 4). | code | 2026-11-25 |

The bulletins lane (addendum 250, #826) queues behind the schema and nflverse PRs and ahead of the projection. The first host reads and the timers' enablement are the architect's blocks. Thursday's migration tag does not carry any of it.

## The ruling, in full (ARCHITECT 2026-11-04 13:05 ET, addendum 252)

> ARCHITECT 2026-11-04 13:05 ET — addendum 252: THE AVAILABILITY RECORD (lane availability-record, new): a bitemporal, append-only store of what was knowable about who plays, stamped by our clock, generalised from the cups' Step B store; two free feeds first (nflverse depth charts, the NHL landing read); a graph projection as step 2, never a record. The operator's direction of 11-04 12:38 ET ("let's go") on my proposal of 12:35.
>
> 0. WHY. Every supplier in the operator's sourcing report (11-04) sells current state or post-hoc history; none preserves what it said before a game. The NHL lane (#105) and the NFL QB term (#427) both stalled on exactly that absence. The fix is ownership: observe early, stamp with our clock, never overwrite — the discipline Step B already lives under (schema.CupLineupObservation: one row per fixture, kickoff and poll; append-only; explicit failed, partial, empty and missed rows; the first complete observation preserved and every later answer its own row). This lane makes that the general store for availability facts in every sport. A season from now we hold a pregame record no vendor sells, and a model term can be built "only from what was readable at or before the cut-off", the cups' rule, in the NHL and the NFL too.
>
> 1. THE MODEL, bitemporal and append-only. Two tables, both created by one migration, both written by ingest commands only, both read mode=ro by everything else:
>    (a) `availability_observations` — one row per fetch: sport; source (a fixed vocabulary, item 3); endpoint (the URL or file name, no secrets); the match_id where the fetch is per game (NULL for a league-wide file), the stored kickoff then; poll_label where polled on a schedule (the probe's T-120 … T-0); scheduled_at; fetched_at (OUR clock, UTC); http_status; payload_sha256; payload_path (the raw answer kept on disk under logs/availability/<source>/<date>/, never under data/, never mirrored); status: complete | partial | empty | failed | missed (Step B's five, the same meanings); late; error (redacted); rows_asserted. NOTHING UPDATES OR DELETES A ROW. A fetch that raised is a row; a poll whose time passed with no call is a row.
>    (b) `availability_assertions` — one row per fact a payload asserted, keyed to its observation: observation_id; sport; kind (a fixed vocabulary: depth_rank | projected_starter | confirmed_starter | eventual_starter | inactive | injury_status | plays_for); player_id (ours, NULL with the source's id beside it when unmapped: source_player_id, player_name verbatim); team_id (ours; NULL + source_team verbatim when unmapped); match_id (NULL for a team-level fact); attrs JSON (pos_abb, pos_slot, pos_rank, status text, the side); source_stamp (THE SOURCE'S OWN TIME for the fact: nflverse's `dt`; NULL where the source gives none — the NHL landing gives none); recorded_at (= the observation's fetched_at, denormalised for the as-of query). No valid_to column and no update: an interval is DERIVED — a fact holds from its observation to the next observation of the same source that asserts the same (kind, player, team[, match]) differently, or that asserts the slot to someone else. "As of T" is one query: the newest observation per source with the chosen clock <= T, and its assertions. That is StackState's time travel in two tables and a WHERE clause.
>    THE TWO CLOCKS, ruled now so no term argues it later: `recorded_at` is OUR knowledge; `source_stamp` is the source's claim. A live-era record, a forward confirmation and a closing-time input use `recorded_at` only (what we had on our disk before the cut-off). A backfilled row (recorded_at later than source_stamp by more than the feed's cadence: nflverse's season file reaches back to its first load, so our first fetch records weeks of history at once) is usable ONLY in a backtest labelled "source-stamped" in its run record and its gate text, never in the live-era record; a term that wants it declares that in its bar. Both clocks are kept on every row so either reading can be audited.
>    Mapping (law 4): a player or team the source names that we cannot map stays NULL with the source's text beside it; mapping is by the existing tables' source ids (players.gsis_id / espn_id where we hold them, nhl player ids as nhl_goalies stores them) and never by name alone; an unmapped row is counted on the ingest's console and in a receipt, never dropped and never guessed.
>
> 2. THE QUERY SURFACE (read-only cli, one command): `availability --sport S --as-of INSTANT [--clock recorded|source] [--match-id N | --team T] [--kind K]` prints the facts in force at the instant under the chosen clock, each with both stamps and its observation; `--history` prints every assertion for the key in time order so a flip shows. The same function is the one a model term, the bulletin's teams section and the Cockpit will read; there is no second path.
>
> 3. THE FEEDS, in order. Each is its own ingest command, its own adapter, its own source vocabulary word, its own fixture tests on saved payloads, and lands as its own PR after the schema PR.
>    (a) nflverse DEPTH CHARTS (source `nflverse_depth_charts`): the release file for the season (github.com/nflverse/nflverse-data, release tag depth_charts, the 2025+ format: dt, team, player_name, espn_id, gsis_id, pos_grp_id, pos_grp, pos_id, pos_name, pos_abb, pos_slot, pos_rank — the dictionary as published; the 2023–2024 weekly files are a DIFFERENT shape and are NOT ingested by this feed: a second adapter later if a backtest wants them, labelled source-stamped). One fetch a day on the host after nflverse's ~07:00 UTC load (a new chain `availability-daily`, timer 08:45 UTC, inside no other chain; UNMETERED; failure receipted and paged as a sync-step failure, stopping nothing). Each fetch is one observation; its NEW rows (dt later than the newest source_stamp we hold for the source) become assertions of kind depth_rank (attrs: pos_grp, pos_abb, pos_slot, pos_rank), one per player-slot; the fetch's payload sha256 is kept, and a fetch whose file is byte-identical to the last is a `complete` observation with rows_asserted 0. Licence CC BY 4.0: the source word carries the attribution, and any output that uses the facts (a bulletin, a page) prints "Depth charts: nflverse (CC BY 4.0)". A QB1 from this feed is a DAILY RANK, not a game-day confirmation (the report's own limit): kind depth_rank says so; nothing here writes projected_starter.
>    (b) THE NHL LANDING READ (source `nhl_api_landing`): per game of the NHL day (the probe's schedule read: GET /v1/schedule/<date>, game types 2 and 3), the landing page at the probe's offsets (T-120, T-90, T-60, T-45, T-35, T-30, T-15, T-0) — each poll an observation with its poll_label — asserting projected_starter per side from matchup.goalieComparison.<side>Team.leaders[0] (playerId, name beside it) EXACTLY as scripts/nhl_leaders_order_receipt.py reads it, and the boxscore at T+20 asserting eventual_starter (the goalie with toi above zero; two in net = two rows, flagged; none = an `empty` observation) — post hoc, kind-labelled, never a pregame fact. The polls run under a watch on the host (an `availability-observe` timer every five minutes, the cup-observe pattern), each poll stamped by our clock; a poll more than five minutes past its time is a `missed` row. The receipt's reading of leaders[0]'s reliability STANDS as read on #105; this feed records what the page asserted and when, which is a fact whatever the page's reliability, and it is the free NHL pregame record from the day it runs.
>    (c) A PAID FEED, IF THE OPERATOR NAMES ONE ON 11-13 (SportsDataIO's Starting Goaltenders by Date is the report's candidate): the same table, source word `sportsdataio_goalies`, kind projected_starter with attrs.confirmed from the response's Confirmed field, polled on the same watch; its adapter is specified with the decision, not before. The 11-13 step's wording stands; what changes is the cost of "none": with (b) running, "none" leaves the NHL lane a free pregame record rather than nothing.
>    THE EVIDENCE RULING (the report's open question, answered): our own stamped observation of a source's response, fetched before the cut-off and kept unaltered (payload sha256, the raw file on disk), IS the pregame evidence. A supplier's assignment timestamp is welcome as source_stamp and never required.
>
> 4. STEP 2, THE GRAPH PROJECTION (after 3(a) and 3(b) are on the host): a nightly rebuild of the record into an EMBEDDED graph engine on the host — file-based, no server, Cypher — nodes Player, Team, Game, Observation; edges from the assertions carrying kind, recorded_at, source_stamp and the derived interval; rebuilt whole from SQLite (mode=ro) by one command, `availability-graph-rebuild`, as the last step of availability-daily; its file under logs/, never under data/, never backed up, never mirrored, deletable without loss. NEVER written by a chain other than its rebuild, NEVER read by the Desk, a prediction, an export or a gate; a failed rebuild is a receipt line and stops nothing. Code's first PR for this step is a one-page comparison of the embedded candidates — name, licence, maintenance state as of the PR's date (that field moved this year; the state is checked, not remembered), Python binding, Cypher dialect, file format — and I pick on it; nothing is installed before the pick. The projection is the lookup and exploration surface (the Cockpit, the bulletins' teams section, my own reads); any feature it suggests is a candidate term that goes through its gate like every other.
>
> 5. WHAT THE LANE NEVER DOES: no model change; no Desk input; no row written to lineups, match_participants, injuries or any existing table (the record is its own two tables; the existing stores are untouched); no provider call from a closing run (the record is read, never fetched, inside a closing); no backdating (a fact recorded after its game is post hoc and labelled so); no deletion ever; no payload under data/; no secret in an endpoint string; no scraping of a source whose terms forbid it (nflverse's licence is explicit; the NHL API is the one we already read; a paid feed's terms come with the decision).
>
> 6. TESTS (the acceptance set): (a) append-only — the ingest commands expose no update or delete path, and a test asserts the tables' row counts only grow across a replay of saved payloads; (b) the as-of query under each clock on a synthetic history with a flip, a backfilled row and a missed poll — the recorded clock never returns the backfilled row before its fetch; (c) the five statuses on saved payloads: complete, partial (a team unmapped), empty, failed (a raised call), missed (a scheduled poll with no call); (d) the nflverse adapter on a saved 2025-format file: every column read by name (law 1), the 2023–2024 shape refused with its reason; (e) the NHL adapter on the probe's saved payloads (the same files the leaders-order receipt reads): leaders[0] per side, two in net, no goalieComparison; (f) a payload with an unmapped player keeps its name and NULL id; (g) the derived interval on a sequence of observations equals the flip the history shows; (h) nothing under data/ after any test.
>
> 7. ORDER AND DATES (a new lane `availability-record` in docs/roadmap.json with these steps; no existing date moves; its Issue filed with the schema PR; the board places it immediately below the model lanes, since the NHL and NFL-QB lanes cannot declare without it — it is the first tooling that unblocks a model lane rather than waits beside one): the schema PR (item 1, the migration, the query command, tests 6(a)–(c), (g), (h)) opens in the next free slot after #825's merge-from-main push and the parity PR — due 11-10; the nflverse feed (3(a), its chain and timer) due 11-12, so the first host observations precede the 11-13 decision; the NHL landing feed (3(b), the watch) due 11-17; the paid adapter, if named, specified 11-14 and due 11-21; the projection's candidate comparison due 11-20, the rebuild due 11-25. The bulletins lane (addendum 250) queues behind the schema and nflverse PRs and ahead of the projection. Each PR body names its commands and arguments; no block ships to the operator; the first host reads and the timers' enablement are my blocks. Thursday's migration tag does not carry any of it.

Dependency Hierarchy: - axios-0.21.4.tgz (Root Library) - :x: **follow-redirects-1.15.9.tgz** (Vulnerable Library)

Found in base branch: main

### Vulnerability Details

follow-redirects is a Node.js HTTP and HTTPS client wrapper that automatically follows redirects. From version 1.16.0 to before version 1.16.1, follow-redirects removes sensitive credential headers (Authorization, Proxy-Authorization, Cookie, and any caller-declared sensitiveHeaders) before following a redirect that crosses to a different host or downgrades to a less secure protocol. The removal routine iterates the caller's headers container with for...in and matches header names against a filter. This assumes the headers container is a plain object keyed by header names. Node's underlying http.request, which follow-redirects is a drop-in replacement for, also accepts headers as an alternating array of names and values. For an array, for...in yields the numeric indices "0", "1", "2" and so on, which never match a header-name filter, so nothing is removed. An application that sends array-form headers and follows an attacker-controlled cross-origin redirect therefore forwards its Authorization, Cookie, and Proxy-Authorization headers verbatim to the attacker-controlled destination, with no error or warning. The sensitiveHeaders option added to fix CVE-2026-40895 / GHSA-r4q5-vmmm-2653 is equally ineffective, because it relies on the same helper. This is an unauthenticated confidentiality vulnerability: any remote server the victim application contacts can harvest the victim's credential headers by responding with a cross-origin redirect. This issue has been patched in version 1.16.1.

C1 Backend — Role-Scoped Operational Work Queues & Query APIs
## Evidence

15 Oct repository audit found **no staff list/read APIs** for operations and Business Workspace reference screens are fixtures only. This is NEW BACKEND query capability; existing [GLO-83](https://linear.app/ahme-hassan/issue/GLO-83/build-hub-operations-console)/223/125 are UI projects, which remain paused.

## Implement ONLY NestJS owner-module API read contracts

* Admin: operational order attention queue, pending decisions, sourcing failures, fulfillment exceptions (small paginated/filterable summaries).
* Supplier: own consolidated PO inbox and line details with own confirmed/ready states; no PII or competitors' prices.
* Hub: assigned location receivable PO lines, per-Order preparation queue, ready shipments, optional assigned dispatch runs.
* Driver: own manifest/details including necessary secured pin/phone/COD and current status; reuse existing driver read API; no duplicate endpoint.
* Cashier/Admin: unsettled expected/declared collections + discrepancies, settlement history scoped to authorized hub.
* Support: case/exception actionable list if existing model permits; use canonical IDs, no independent state ownership.
* Use typed DTOs, bounded pagination, whitelisted sorting/filters, role+resource ownership checks, stable consistent statuses, no new denormalized parallel source of truth unless measured necessary.

## DoD

API documentation and role-by-role HTTP/DB tests show each actor sees its own work only; Driver B/Supplier B/Hub B denied cross-tenant/foreign records, PII minimized. No Next.js, dashboard layouts, auth UI, live SSE or generic reporting engine.

So I put together this OpenProject Agent Engine. It auto assigns the 'work package' (ticket), then kicks off the agent to do the work.

If it passes, the PR gets merged and and ticket is closed. If it doesn't pass, it gets kicked back to the original agent to fix the issues. Feedback welcome and hope it can help someone. Execute Workflow node panel shows stale sub-workflow restriction state after changing the selected sub-workflow
### Bug Description

When opening an Execute Workflow node panel and selecting or switching the target sub-workflow, the restriction callout inside the node panel does not force a fresh policy check if the sub-workflow was already checked earlier in the session or if the workflow ID field started empty. If a sub-workflow's restricted node policies were updated since the workflow editor loaded, the node panel continues displaying the cached restriction state instead of fetching the current check.

### To Reproduce

1. Open a workflow containing an Execute Workflow node that points to Sub-Workflow A (or starts with an empty workflow ID), and also have Sub-Workflow B checked on the canvas.
2. Update Sub-Workflow B so it now contains (or no longer contains) a policy-restricted node.
3. Open the Execute Workflow node panel and change the selected sub-workflow to Sub-Workflow B.
4. Observe that no new sub-workflow policy check request is sent for Sub-Workflow B, and the callout in the node panel reflects the old cached state.

### Expected behavior

Selecting or changing the target sub-workflow inside the open Execute Workflow node panel should always fetch a fresh sub-workflow policy check for the newly selected sub-workflow.

22.14.0

main (default)

source_text:
PROC-STRATEGY-001: optimize ex-ante flexible and backup capacity commitments
## Purpose

Build the first-stage decision layer above [#5099 static portfolio sourcing](https://github.com/Luminous-Dynamics/mycelix/pull/5099) and [#5108 adaptive recourse](https://github.com/Luminous-Dynamics/mycelix/pull/5108): choose which flexible/backup options to pre-commit, and how much reserved capacity to purchase, before disruption occurs.

This is a research/reference optimization task. It is not contract execution, supplier outreach, spend authorization, or a live purchasing system.

## Architecture split

- **Static portfolio layer (#5099):** chooses a normal/base supplier allocation.
- **Recourse layer (#5108):** given a fixed baseline and a fixed set of already-committed options, computes scenario-specific on-time recovery under explicit constraints.
- **This issue:** selects the option set/capacity before scenarios are realized, then evaluates the same committed plan across the frozen scenario set using #5108 semantics.

Keep these layers separable for differential tests; first-stage selection must not call a live authority or treat scenario probabilities as known by default.

## Paradigm shift

Move from "buy a backup supplier" to "price the option value of flexible capacity and standby recovery." An option is valuable only when its capacity, qualification, activation lead, transit time, common-cause dependencies, fees and scenario coverage make recovery feasible.

## Required decision variables and constraints

- Which pre-qualified flexible/backup options to commit.
- How much capacity to reserve per option, respecting minimums/increments and shared capacity-pool ceilings.
- Upfront retainer/option fees, activation fees, unit costs and transport costs.
- Baseline allocation + reserved contingency capacity must respect capacity accounting without double pledging the same pool.
- Minimum service-level target (optional, versioned) and total budget.
- Scenario-by-scenario feasible recourse and on-time recovery; no supplier capacity may be activated twice across conflicting commitments.
- Failure-domain overlap across supplier parent, plant, critical sub-tier, utility, route, port and geography.
- Exact evidence freshness, qualification, quote and option validity.

## Optimization semantics

Initially, use a bounded exact first-stage enumerator for very small cases. Evaluate each candidate commitment set by invoking an independently implemented second-stage recourse oracle—not by asking a candidate set to score itself. Compare strategies across cost, worst-case shortage, scenario-level shortage distribution and coverage.

If disruption probabilities are uncalibrated, use declared scenarios and worst-case envelopes rather than expected-cost claims. If a probability model is later admitted, bind its source, training/calibration window, version, uncertainty set and out-of-sample qualification evidence.

Do not force all trade-offs into an unversioned scalar. A policy may apply explicit feasibility constraints and a declared lexicographic objective, or present a Pareto frontier for authorized human/policy selection.

## Required baselines

1. No flexible/backup capacity.
2. Cheapest backup-only contract.
3. Flexible-only contract.
4. Backup-only contract.
5. Greedy “reserve the cheapest capacity first.”
6. Exhaustive joint first-/second-stage optimum on tractable cases.

Every strategy uses the exact same frozen input and scenario manifest.

## Independent verifier and adversarial cases

- Capacity promised to normal supply is also sold as backup.
- Multiple offer IDs share one capacity pool or supplier parent.
- Flexible/backup capacity exists but activation plus transit misses the deadline.
- Option fee is sunk even when the option is unused.
- A reserve is already committed to another request.
- A backup supplier is hit by the same plant/port/utility/sub-tier disruption as the base source.
- Quote, qualification, or capacity evidence expires before scenario execution.
- Model chooses a cheap option but exceeds total budget after activation fees.
- A generated scenario is accidentally treated as a calibrated probability.
- Search bounds are exceeded but a partial plan is labelled optimal.
- Candidate order changes an exact tie.
- An option set meets nominal demand but fails all severe disruption cases.

## Proposed benchmarks (not measured)

- Exact agreement with independent exhaustive oracle for every tractable first-stage/recourse instance.
- Zero shared-capacity overcommitment, invalid option activation, deadline violation or budget breach.

- Report cost regret versus the exact optimum on tractable instances and gap/unknown status on larger instances.
- At least 10,000 generated micro-instances after the first independent oracle passes.
- Measure p50/p95/max runtime and memory on named pinned hardware before setting performance promises.

## Research references

- Dai, Zou & Zhang (2026), robust supplier selection/order allocation using normal, flexible and backup modes: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijpe.2026.110060
- Li, Doan & Branke (online 2026/preprint), distributionally robust sourcing under uncertain disruption impact: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijpe.2026.110160
- Hosseini et al. (2019), reactive restoration and disruption dependencies: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijpe.2019.03.018

These papers motivate comparable experiments; reported gains are not expected results for Mycelix.

## Claim ceiling

No live supplier contact, purchase orders, contract amendments, inventory mutations, payment execution, dispatch or legal-conformity claim. Start with synthetic civilian maintenance supplies, repairable IT equipment, food essentials and community infrastructure.
