Computer use: fill in a form with tricky fields and see how it handles errors
Check how the agent copes with date pickers, dropdowns, uploads and validation errors.

## Try this

1. Find a public practice form made for testing, with a date picker, dropdowns, a file upload and required fields (search "practice form for automation testing").
2. Ask the agent to fill it in with made-up details you give it, and stop before the final submit.
3. Give it one value the form will reject, such as a bad email or a date in the past.
4. Ask it to change one field, then submit (on the practice site only).

## What to look for

- Each field gets the value you gave, including the date picker and dropdowns.
- It notices a validation error and fixes it, or asks you.
- It stops before submitting when you told it to.
- Its screenshots show the filled form.

Only submit practice forms. Never send real forms with made-up details.

## Your report

Post one comment here with:

- Links to your threads (`app.useagent.org/session/...`)
- What worked
- What broke or confused you, and what you expected instead
- Screenshots or a short screen recording

Open a separate bug issue for anything broken, with the steps to reproduce it, and link it in your comment.

No need to claim; post your report as a comment.

---

**General asks**
- Do the steps yourself in the hosted app. Sign up with your email at [app.useagent.org](https://app.useagent.org/login?ref=feedback); you don't need an API key or a card to start. The link in the sign-up email works for 24 hours, so check spam if it's missing.
- Run everything by hand. Reports from runs done or simulated by another AI tool get closed.
- Use made-up details, test accounts and data you own. Don't point the agent at other people's accounts, inboxes or private data, and don't send real forms or messages to strangers.
- More than one person can report on the same issue, and every report helps. If someone already found what you found, add only what's different.
- Stuck? Comment here with a screenshot and we'll help.

**Keep private details out of here**

This page is public. Don't post your real email, phone number, address, API keys, or screenshots that show any of them; blur them first. Send anything private to **hi@useagent.org** with a link to your comment here.

**Using AI tools, and what gets no reply**
- AI help is fine. Blind AI output is not. You must understand every line you submit, run it yourself, and show it working in the app with your own screenshots or recording.
- Pull requests that look generated and untested get closed without a reply and labeled `spam`, which also means they don't count for Hacktoberfest. Signs we look for: no proof from a real run, code that ignores this repo's patterns or reinvents helpers that already exist, unrelated files changed, a description that only restates the issue, and failing checks nobody looked at.
- One pull request per issue, by the person who claimed it. Opening pull requests on issues someone else has taken, or several near-identical pull requests for the same bounty, counts as farming and gets the same treatment.
- Bounties are paid only for the verified outcome the issue describes (for example, a workshop that actually happened, or an app that works on both systems), never for a write-up, a plan, or an unfinished attempt.
- When we ask a question in review, answer it in your own words. If you can't explain your change, we can't merge it.

Could you investigate whether this is a mobile frontend compatibility issue or a problem with the hosted chat assets on my Cloud instance?

I can provide the affected Chat URLs and screenshots.

I have five Fiverr accounts forwarding their notification emails to one central Gmail inbox. This inbox is connected to an n8n Gmail Trigger configured to check for new emails every minute. The trigger detects some incoming Fiverr notifications, but other emails are not detected consistently. This happens even though the emails are successfully delivered to the central Gmail inbox. The issue affects the reliability of my Fiverr notification automation. ## Additional Context I have two separate email notification automations running on the same self-hosted n8n instance: one for Upwork and another for Fiverr. Both automations use the same approach: - Gmail Trigger node to monitor incoming emails. - AI processing to analyze and classify notifications. - Slack integration to send notifications. The Upwork automation works perfectly. Whenever I receive a new Upwork email, the Gmail Trigger detects it, processes it, and successfully sends a notification to Slack. However, the Fiverr automation does not behave the same way. Although it uses a similar workflow structure and configuration, it inconsistently detects incoming Fiverr emails. Some notifications reach Slack, while others are completely missed. Since both automations run on the same n8n instance and use the same Gmail Trigger approach, I would like to understand why the Fiverr workflow is not detecting emails reliably while the Upwork workflow works as expected. ### Current Configuration - Gmail Trigger polling interval: 1 minute - Simple: Disabled (`false`) - Maximum results: 10 - Gmail search query: `from:(fiverr)` (tested with and without this filter) ### To Reproduce 1. Set up a Gmail account that receives forwarded emails from multiple Fiverr accounts. 2. Connect the Gmail account to an n8n Gmail Trigger node. 3. Configure the trigger to poll every minute. 4. Send or receive multiple test emails through the forwarding accounts. 5. Compare the emails received in Gmail with the emails detected by the Gmail Trigger. 6. Observe that some emails are detected while others are missed. ### Expected behavior The Gmail Trigger should reliably detect all new emails matching its configured search criteria during subsequent polling cycles. Emails successfully delivered to the connected Gmail inbox should not be silently missed. ### Debug Info ### Operating System Ubuntu (Hostinger VPS) ### n8n Version 2.45.6 ### Node.js Version Unknown ### Database SQLite (default) ### Execution mode own (deprecated) ### Hosting self hosted

Array .min() and .max() throw 'Maximum call stack size exceeded' on large arrays
### Bug Description

`Array.min()` and `Array.max()` in expressions throw `Maximum call stack size exceeded` for an array of about 125,000 numbers or more.

Both functions call `Math.min(...value)` / `Math.max(...value)`, which passes every element of the array as a separate function argument. V8 (and QuickJS) put those arguments on the stack, so a large enough array overflows it. `sum()` and `average()` use `reduce` and work on the same arrays.

The same code is in `packages/workflow/src/extensions/array-extensions.ts` and its mirror in `@n8n/expression-runtime`.

### To Reproduce

1. Add a Set (Edit Fields) node with an expression such as `{{ Array.from({ length: 200000 }, (_, i) => i).max() }}`, or call `.min()`/`.max()` on a large numeric array from an earlier node (e.g. `{{ $json.prices.max() }}` with 200,000 prices).
2. Execute the node.
3. The expression fails with `Maximum call stack size exceeded`.

Minimal Node reproduction of the same call:

```sh
node -e 'console.log(Math.max(...new Array(200000).fill(1)))'
# RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
```

### Expected behavior

`199999`, as for smaller arrays. `.sum()` on the same array already works.

### Debug Info

Found by reading the code on `master`, and reproduced with tests that call `.min()`/`.max()` on a 200,000-element array in the legacy and QuickJS expression engines and on `arrayExtensions.functions.min/max` directly.

### Operating System

Ubuntu Linux

### n8n Version

master (current HEAD)

### Node.js Version

20.19.2

### Database

SQLite (default)

### Execution mode

main (default)

### Hosting

self hosted

Show HN: Evaluate and improve your agent steering
Hi HN, excited to be open sourcing two tools that we have built over past few months which helps to understand your own work with AI coding agents Agent Desk is a local macOS app which allows you to browse your sessions across all top coding agents - Claude code, cursor, codex, github copilot, Kiro, Antigravity. You can find sessions by your projects, revisit those conversations, understand and inspect your entire harness - rules, skills, hooks, subagents.  https://github.com/tetriz-ai/agent-desk  Session Intelligence is a go library which helps structure and analyse your session transcripts using your own LLM. It can help understand missing context, repeated corrections, if session reached its goal and where is effort being wasted. It can also surface leaked credentials and PII.  https://github.com/tetriz-ai/session-intelligence  Both are MIT-licensed. You can also combine both together and understanding your agent steering habits better. Excited about the community using it.

Two readings, and they are not the same postulate:

- **Ironic register** — saying the opposite of what is meant, with the audience expected to hear the inversion. A real and common rhetorical move.

Your counter-counter-postulate needs the second. The second needs *tone*. And tone is exactly what a machine transcript strips first. Which produces the structural problem in one line:

> The hypothesis is about how something was said, and the only surviving record is of *what* was said.

That is not a reason to dismiss it. It is a reason to notice that it cannot be scored from the artifact you have, and to ask what *would* score it — the audio, ideally the video, and the ad log for that hour.

# 2. The wording does settle one narrow question, and it cuts against plain dishonesty

Read the modal:

> "So it **had to** cost a lot of money because it's, you know, it's a full color heavy paper mailer."

**"Had to"** is an epistemic modal of inference, not of knowledge. Compare the alternatives a speaker with inside information would use: "it cost a lot," "they spent a fortune," "I know what that costs." Each asserts. "It had to cost" *deduces* — from the same surface features you and I have been reasoning from: full colour, heavy stock, saturation.

So on the one question the text can answer: **Beck is not claiming knowledge of the spend. He is performing an inference, and marking it as an inference.** The disfluencies ("you know," "I mean") sit in the same place, hedging the claim rather than asserting it.

An inference is not a lie. It can be a bad inference, a self-serving one, or a performed one — but the grammatical form he chose is the form of a man reasoning aloud from a mailer, not a man reporting a fact he holds.

Which means the honest version of your postulate is not "Beck isn't speaking honestly." It's **"Beck doesn't know, and is filling the gap with a plausible inference — the same one the audience would make."** That's a different and much more defensible claim, and it's the one his own grammar supports.

Proposal: global supplier catalogue from free sources (CoE results + Open Supply Hub + Trase), after the trip
**Decision needed:** approve a global supplier catalogue, built from free sources we're allowed to use, after the trip-critical work (#13 → #8 → #10 → #9). **Recommendation: approve, but build it after Jan 17.** This answers your question on #8 about where the data would come from.

## Problem / opportunity
The Sourcing CRM starts with 41 Costa Rican organisations. A roaster or importer sourcing from Colombia, Ethiopia or Brazil starts with an empty list, and no free worldwide producer registry exists. The research found three sources we're allowed to use. Together they cover top farms, plus co-ops, mills and exporters, in about 17 origins.

## Proposed feature (what Z will see and be able to do)
- **Load suppliers** in the Sourcing tab, by origin (multi-select). It adds source-linked, *unverified* organisations, the same way the Costa Rica seed works. Loading twice never duplicates.
- Each organisation shows its **source and license** and keeps `verified = no` until you mark it.
- On every organisation, **Check certificate** links open the Fairtrade (FLOCERT) and Rainforest Alliance public searches pre-filled with its name. Nothing is copied from them.

## Approach (files touched, data sources + their terms, new dependencies)
- **Cup of Excellence results** (ACE public results pages, about 17 origins, 1999–2026): hand-curated facts per lot (farm, producer, region, rank, score, auction $/lb) with a link back. This matches the Costa Rica seed and ACE's guidance. We won't use ACE's Farm Directory, which is for members only.
- **Open Supply Hub coffee locations** (co-ops, mills, warehouses, exporters; **CC BY-SA 4.0**): a coffee extract downloaded by hand from the free web tier, stored in its own file `app/crm/seed_osh_coffee.json` with attribution. The README data-source table will note that this file is CC BY-SA, not MIT. We won't use the paid API.
- **Trase coffee exporters** (2020, 10 producing countries): only if the Zenodo license turns out to be open. I'll check that first and drop the source if it isn't.
- New `source_license` field in `app/crm/schema.py`, and per-country seed loading in `service.seed()`. No new dependencies and no scraping.
- Rejected alternative: scraping national registries or certification databases. None offers a feed, and their terms are unclear or restrictive.

## Out of scope
Personal contact details (never seeded), paid customs or shipment data (it would improve quality, but we won't wire it in), and auto-refresh (a manual yearly refresh is fine).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Load by origin, idempotent; every record has a source link and license and `verified = no`
- [ ] The README data-source table lists each source with its terms, including the CC BY-SA note for the OS Hub file
- [ ] Certificate links on the organisation page
- [ ] ruff + pytest pass; demo-mode curl smoke test

## Size: M (2 runs). Build after #10 and #9, ideally after the trip.

Turnkey PCBA vs. Consignment PCBA: Which PCB Assembly Service Is Right for Your Business? - Hitech Circuits
Frequently Asked Questions About Turnkey and Consignment PCBA
Is turnkey PCBA better than consignment PCBA?
Neither option is universally better. Turnkey PCBA may suit businesses seeking integrated material sourcing and assembly, while consignment PCBA may suit customers that prefer to purchase and manage their own components.

Is consignment PCBA always cheaper?
No. Although the assembly quotation may exclude component procurement, the customer must also account for purchasing costs, logistics, inventory handling, and material coordination. The total project cost depends on the specific requirements and purchasing arrangements.

Can I supply some components and ask the manufacturer to source the rest?
In many cases, a partial consignment arrangement may be possible. The customer and supplier should agree on which materials will be supplied by each party, how the materials will be identified, and how shortages will be handled.

Does turnkey PCBA include functional testing?
Not necessarily. Functional testing depends on the supplier's service scope and the customer's requirements. Firmware, test fixtures, programming, and acceptance criteria may need to be provided or quoted separately.

What files are needed for turnkey PCBA?
Commonly required files include a BOM, Gerber files, pick-and-place data, assembly drawings, order quantity, and testing requirements.

How can I get a quotation for PCB assembly?
Prepare the available manufacturing files and specify the order quantity, testing requirements, and preferred material supply model. A PCBA supplier can then review the project and clarify any additional information needed for quotation.

Conclusion
Choosing between turnkey PCBA and consignment PCBA requires a clear understanding of purchasing responsibilities, material availability, production coordination, and total manufacturing costs.

Turnkey PCBA can simplify supply chain management by coordinating component sourcing and assembly through one supplier. Consignment PCBA gives customers greater direct control over component procurement and may be suitable when they already have the required materials or established purchasing arrangements.

The right choice depends on your project requirements, internal resources, and production strategy.

source_text:
Custom Tablecloth Styles: Throw, Fitted, Stretch, and Runner Covers
A table is more than a place to put brochures or products. At a trade show, market, conference, or corporate event, it is part of the first impression. A branded cloth can make the station easier to recognize, hide visual clutter, and connect the tabletop to the rest of the display. The right style depends on how the table will be used, how much of it needs to be covered, and whether you prefer a relaxed drape or a close, tailored fit. The broader[ SignageBuzz Canada event-display collection](https://www.signagebuzz.ca/) can help you think about the table as one part of the complete setup.
This guide compares four common custom tablecloth styles: the traditional throw, the fitted cover, the stretch cover, and the table runner. The[ SignageBuzz custom tablecloth collection](https://www.signagebuzz.ca/custom-tablecloths) describes these formats for branded event setups, with rectangular table options commonly organized around 4-foot, 6-foot, and 8-foot tables. Use the comparison below as a planning guide, then confirm the exact measurements and configuration for the product you select.
What Are the Main Custom Tablecloth Styles?
The four styles serve different visual and practical purposes:
•Throw cover: A loose cloth that drapes over the table and creates a classic event look.
•Fitted cover: A tailored cover shaped to the table, with a neater, more structured silhouette.
•Stretch cover: A tensioned fabric cover that pulls close to the tabletop and legs for a sleek appearance.
•Runner cover: A branded strip placed over a plain tablecloth or venue-provided table covering.
Some suppliers use “tablecloth,” “table cover,” and “table throw” interchangeably. The important distinction is how the fabric sits on the table. A throw leaves more room for variation, while fitted and stretch formats require closer attention to the table’s actual dimensions. A runner provides a branding layer without replacing the base cover.
1. Throw Tablecloths: The Traditional, Flexible Option
A throw, also called a standard or loose table cover, drapes over the tabletop and down the sides. It is the familiar choice for trade-show tables, registration desks, school events, vendor booths, and corporate presentations. The[ standard table cover range](https://www.signagebuzz.ca/standard-table-covers) lists 4-foot, 6-foot, and 8-foot rectangular formats, with three-sided and four-sided coverage options.
Why choose a throw?
The main advantage is flexibility. A loose cover can accommodate small differences between tables that are nominally the same size. That can matter when an event organizer supplies the furniture or when a team uses tables from more than one venue. The soft drape also creates a conventional, approachable look that suits many brands.
A three-sided throw keeps the back open. Staff can sit behind the table and reach stored materials more easily. A four-sided throw covers the back as well, producing a more complete branded appearance and helping conceal boxes or spare supplies.
What to watch for
A throw can bunch at the corners or move more easily than a fitted style. Smooth the front before visitors arrive, and keep the hem away from walkways. If wind is a concern, ask the supplier which construction is appropriate and secure the table and display according to venue rules. A tablecloth should not be treated as an anchoring system.
2. Fitted Tablecloths: A Clean, Tailored Silhouette
A fitted cover is cut and sewn to follow the shape of a particular table. Instead of hanging loosely, it creates a closer profile with defined corners. The[ fitted table cover page](https://www.signagebuzz.ca/custom-tablecloths/fitted-table-covers) lists three-sided, four-sided, and four-sided-with-zipper configurations for rectangular tables in several sizes.
Why choose a fitted cover?
Fitted covers are a strong choice when a polished, architectural appearance matters. The closer fit keeps the front and sides visually controlled, which is useful when the table will be photographed or viewed from multiple directions. Full coverage can also keep stored items out of sight, while a three-sided version preserves rear access.
A zippered configuration can provide a practical access point without leaving the entire back open. Consider how staff will retrieve literature, samples, or personal items before choosing the configuration.
What to watch for
A fitted cover is less forgiving of measurement errors than a loose throw. Confirm the table length, depth, height, corner shape, and any unusual legs or frame parts. A venue’s “6-foot table” may not match the dimensions of a table owned by your organization. If you are buying a complete table-and-cover solution, a[ folding table with fitted table cover](https://www.signagebuzz.ca/folding-table-with-fitted-table-cover) can simplify the matching process.
3. Stretch Tablecloths: A Sleek, Tensioned Look
A stretch cover uses elastic fabric to create a taut silhouette around the table. Rather than relying on a loose drop, the material is pulled into place so the front and sides look smooth and close to the structure. This style suits brands that want a contemporary, streamlined presentation.
The[ stretch table cover page](https://www.signagebuzz.ca/custom-tablecloths/stretch-table-covers) is the relevant product destination for this format. Because stretch covers depend on tension, accurate table measurements are especially important. Check the table’s length, depth, height, leg position, and base shape before ordering.
Why choose a stretch cover?
A stretch cover can reduce visible loose fabric and create a strong modern outline. It works well for technology demonstrations, premium product displays, contemporary conferences, and booths where a crisp visual system matters. It can also be useful when the table will be seen from the sides and the brand wants consistent coverage around the structure.
What to watch for
Do not assume that a stretch cover will fit every table labelled with the same nominal size. Fixed feet, unusual legs, thick tabletops, or a different table depth can affect the result. Allow enough time for a careful proof and fit check, especially when the table is supplied by the venue.
4. Table Runners: Focused Branding with Less Coverage
A runner is a long branded strip placed over the centre of a table. It can sit on a plain tablecloth, a neutral solid-color base, or a venue-provided cover. The[ custom table runner page](https://www.signagebuzz.ca/table-runner) describes 300D polyester runners with full-colour dye-sublimation printing and rectangular table formats.
Why choose a runner?
A runner is useful when you want a visible logo or message without replacing the entire table covering. It is also practical for organizations that already own neutral tablecloths or need to update campaigns more often than they replace their base covers. Different runners can support different events while the underlying cloth remains consistent.
A runner can create a lighter visual treatment, leaving space for brochures, samples, or products on either side. It is also easier to coordinate with a table that does not match a standard trade-show size, although you should still check the length, width, and desired overhang.
What to watch for
Do not place the primary message where products will cover it. Decide whether the runner should hang over the front and back, over the ends, or finish near the tabletop edge. The source category guidance describes runners as commonly 24 to 36 inches wide, with a 6- to 12-inch overhang often used for a traditional setup; treat those figures as planning guidance and confirm the actual product dimensions before ordering.
Throw vs. Fitted vs. Stretch vs. Runner: A Quick Comparison
A throw is usually the most forgiving option when table dimensions may vary. A fitted cover is better when you want a tailored shape and can confirm the measurements. A stretch cover emphasizes a tight, contemporary silhouette and needs careful fit planning. A runner is the lightest branding option and works best when the table already has a suitable base.
Think of the decision as a balance between coverage, fit, access, and visual style. A four-sided throw or fitted cover gives more complete concealment. A three-sided version makes rear access easier. A stretch cover prioritizes a close appearance. A runner prioritizes flexibility and a smaller branding footprint.
How to Choose the Right Style
Start with the table, not the artwork
Measure the actual table you will use. Record its length, depth, height, tabletop thickness, corner profile, and leg placement. If the table comes from a venue, request the specifications before designing the artwork. A fitted or stretch cover should not be ordered from a rough estimate.
If you are working in a compact booth, compare the table with the rest of the display. A[ 10-foot trade-show display](https://www.signagebuzz.ca/trade-show-displays/10ft-displays) may provide a larger visual backdrop, while the tablecloth handles lower-level branding and storage concealment.
Decide how much access you need
Choose three-sided coverage when staff need easy access behind the table or when the back is against a wall. Choose four-sided coverage when the table may be viewed from behind or when hidden storage is important. For a runner, plan where staff will stand and where brochures or products will sit so the logo remains visible.
Match the style to the venue
Indoor conferences often allow more control over the setup. Outdoor markets add wind, rain, damp ground, and uneven surfaces to the planning process. A branded[ custom pop-up tent](https://www.signagebuzz.ca/custom-pop-up-tents) can provide overhead shelter, but the tent, table, and any display accessories still need appropriate anchoring and safe placement.
For a round or cocktail-height table, use a cover made for that shape rather than forcing a rectangular cloth into place. For a portable check-in or sampling station, a complete table-and-cover kit may be more practical than sourcing each component separately.
Consider packing and repeat use
The best style is one your team can install, remove, clean, fold, and store consistently. A loose throw may be quick to position. A fitted cover may require more attention to corners and zippers. A stretch cover needs careful handling so the fabric is not caught on sharp hardware. A runner is easy to swap when campaigns change, but it still needs a clean, dry storage method.
Design and Branding Advice
Keep the front panel simple
Visitors usually see the front first. Put the logo, organization name, or short descriptor in a location that remains visible when the table is loaded. Keep important text away from seams, corners, zippers, and areas that fold over the edge.
One strong logo and one concise message are usually more useful than a paragraph of copy. If the cover will support lead generation, use a short call to action only when it can be read quickly from several feet away.
Design for the whole format
A throw, fitted cover, and stretch cover may expose the front, sides, and sometimes the back. Check how the artwork wraps around corners. A runner has a narrower visual area, so reserve clear space for the central logo and avoid placing critical information near the ends.
Use the artwork template for the exact style and size. Product pages may list accepted file types and preferred formats, but the correct template is the best way to check panel orientation, bleed, and safe areas.
Coordinate the table with the rest of the booth
A cover should support the booth rather than compete with it. Pair a strong table graphic with a restrained backdrop, or use a simpler cover when the back wall already carries a large campaign message. For a larger fabric system, review[ portable 8-foot display options](https://www.signagebuzz.ca/trade-show-displays/8ft-displays) and[ tension fabric display options](https://www.signagebuzz.ca/trade-show-booths/tension-fabric-displays), then keep colour, logo scale, and message hierarchy consistent.
Outdoor brands may also coordinate the table with[ straight flags](https://www.signagebuzz.ca/straight-flags/) or a canopy. Repeat the logo and key colours, but do not duplicate every line of copy on every surface.
Venue and Setup Considerations
Before the event, confirm whether the venue supplies a 4-foot, 6-foot, 8-foot, round, or cocktail table. Ask about table height, depth, placement, power access, aisle clearance, and rules for stored materials. Some venues may request documentation for fire resistance or other material requirements. Verify the exact product documentation and the venue’s current rules rather than assuming that a general material description is sufficient.
At setup, put the cover on before placing heavy items on the tabletop. Smooth the front, check that corners are seated correctly, and keep the hem or runner away from walking paths. Store boxes under the table only when the venue permits it, and keep staff access clear.
For an outdoor setup, check the forecast and have a plan for wind and moisture. A waterproof or water-resistant fabric description does not make the whole display weatherproof. Protect printed fabric from sharp edges, allow damp material to dry fully, and store it clean and dry after the event.
If the table is part of a larger branded environment, a[ 10x10 event kit with a printed table cover](https://www.signagebuzz.ca/10x10-trade-show-kit-full-walls-printed-table-cover) can help coordinate the table with walls and other display elements. A[ 10x10 deluxe event booth kit](https://www.signagebuzz.ca/10x10-deluxe-event-booth-kit-walls-flag-table) offers another package format to compare, while a[ 10x15 package with a table cover](https://www.signagebuzz.ca/10x15-pop-up-logo-tent-table-cover) serves the same planning purpose for a larger footprint. Review what is included in any package before assuming that a table, cover, or carrying case is part of the order.
Best Uses for Each Style
•Throw: General trade shows, conferences, registration desks, school events, and vendor tables where flexibility matters.
•Fitted: Corporate booths, information counters, photographed displays, and settings where a tailored appearance is important.
•Stretch: Modern product demonstrations, technology events, premium promotions, and setups viewed from several angles.
•Runner: Retail counters, campaign refreshes, sponsor tables, and organizations that already own a plain base cover.
A style can work in more than one setting. The best match comes from the combination of table shape, staff workflow, visitor movement, branding goals, and venue rules.
Custom Tablecloth Checklist
Before ordering, confirm the following:
•Measure the exact length, depth, height, and shape of the table.
•Confirm whether the table is rectangular, round, or cocktail height.
•Choose a throw, fitted, stretch, or runner format.
•Decide between three-sided and four-sided coverage where offered.
•Confirm rear access needs and under-table storage plans.
•Check the product’s material, care instructions, and intended use.
•Review venue rules for fire documentation, table coverage, and aisle clearance.
•Use the artwork template for the exact size and construction.
•Keep key text away from seams, corners, zippers, and folded edges.
•Approve the proof for spelling, colours, orientation, and panel placement.
•Plan how the cover will be packed, transported, cleaned, dried, and stored.
•Bring a setup plan for outdoor wind, rain, uneven ground, or changing conditions.
Frequently Asked Questions
1. What is the difference between a throw and a fitted tablecloth?
A throw drapes loosely over the table, while a fitted cover is shaped more closely to the table dimensions. A throw offers more flexibility; a fitted cover creates a more tailored silhouette.
2. Is a stretch tablecloth the same as a fitted tablecloth?
No. Both can look close to the table, but a stretch cover relies on tensioned fabric, while a fitted cover uses a sewn shape designed for the table. Confirm the construction and fit requirements for the specific product.
3. Which tablecloth style is best for trade shows?
It depends on the table and the desired look. A throw is versatile, a fitted cover looks structured, a stretch cover looks modern, and a runner works when a plain base already exists.
4. Should I choose a three-sided or four-sided cover?
Choose three-sided coverage when staff need rear access or seating space. Choose four-sided coverage when you want fuller concealment and branding around the table.
5. Can I use a runner without a full tablecloth?
You can, but the result depends on the table surface and venue expectations. A runner is usually intended to add branding over a plain tablecloth or another suitable base.
6. What table sizes are commonly available?
The cited SignageBuzz rectangular pages organize options around 4-foot, 6-foot, and 8-foot tables. Always confirm the exact finished dimensions and product configuration before ordering.
7. How do I measure for a fitted or stretch cover?
Measure the actual table length, depth, height, tabletop thickness, corners, and leg placement. Share unusual features with the supplier before selecting a close-fitting cover.
8. Can a rectangular cover be used on a round table?
It is not recommended for a polished result. The hem will not follow the table shape evenly. Select a cover designed for the table’s shape.
9. Where should the logo go on a tablecloth?
Place the primary logo on the front panel where it will remain visible above products and literature. Check side panels as well if visitors will approach from multiple directions.
10. How much text should go on a custom table cover?
Keep it brief. A logo, organization name, short descriptor, or concise call to action is usually easier to read than a paragraph, especially in a busy event aisle.
11. Can I use the same artwork on a throw, fitted cover, and stretch cover?
You may be able to reuse the brand elements, but the layout should be adapted to each construction. Seams, corners, zippers, and tension can change how artwork appears.
12. Are custom tablecloths suitable for outdoor events?
Some products describe water-resistant or waterproof and UV-related features, but outdoor suitability varies by product and conditions. Confirm the exact construction and secure the entire setup for wind.
13. What should I do if the venue supplies the table?
Ask for the table’s exact dimensions and shape in advance. If the venue cannot confirm them, a more flexible throw or a runner may be easier to plan than a fitted or stretch cover.
14. How should I store a printed tablecloth?
Remove debris, follow the product’s care instructions, and let the fabric dry completely before folding. Keep it away from sharp or abrasive hardware during transport and storage.
15. Can a table runner support a seasonal campaign?
Yes. A runner can make it easier to change the message while keeping a neutral base cover in service. Check that the new runner fits the table and leaves the artwork visible.
16. Should the back of the table be covered?
Cover the back when the table can be viewed from behind or when you want to conceal stored items. Leave it open when staff access, seating, or quick storage retrieval is more important.
17. Does the tablecloth include the table?
Not necessarily. Many cover and runner listings are for the printed fabric only. Read the package contents carefully, especially when comparing a cover with a complete table-and-cover kit.
18. What should I check before approving the proof?
Check spelling, logo proportions, colours, panel orientation, seams, corners, zipper areas, and the relationship between the artwork and the selected table size. Confirm that the proof matches the product configuration you intend to buy.
Conclusion
Throw, fitted, stretch, and runner covers each solve a different event-display problem. Choose a throw for flexible, traditional coverage; a fitted cover for a crisp tailored profile; a stretch cover for a sleek tensioned look; or a runner for focused branding over an existing tablecloth. Start with the actual table, decide how staff will use the space, and design the visible panels for quick reading. With the right fit and a clear proof, your table can become a practical, consistent part of the entire branded setup.

source_text:
Allocation edge cases leave orders stuck or over-allocated
Found during the docs review (#96). Each was read from the code; none has a test.

**1. An order allocated entirely by hand never reaches suppliers.**
- Allocating every line from the supplier list (`CreatePurchaseOrderItemHandler` → `OrderItemAllocator::forOrderItem`) creates the PO items as PENDING.
- PO items only move to PROCESSING at the end of an `OrderAllocator::process()` run that started with something outstanding (`OrderAllocator.php`, `allItemsAllocated()` → `updateItemStatus()`).
- After a full manual allocation, clicking Allocate returns "No items to allocate." (`AllocateOrderHandler`) and changes nothing.
- `app:build-purchase-orders` only picks orders with no PO yet (`CustomerOrderDoctrineRepository`), and acceptance only reads PROCESSING POs.
- The order stays Pending until someone sets each PO item to Processing by hand.

**2. A cancelled order item still counts as outstanding.**
- An item can only be cancelled while nothing is on a PO, so its outstanding quantity is its full quantity.
- `getOutstandingQty()` doesn't look at the item's own status (`CustomerOrderItem.php`), and `OrderAllocator::process()` doesn't skip cancelled items.
- So Allocate can put a cancelled line on a PO. If no supplier has the stock, the order reports "Cannot allocate all items" for ever.

**3. Rewind can over-allocate a line.**
- `PurchaseOrder::forceRewindToPending()` sets every item to PENDING, including REFUNDED and CANCELLED ones.
- A refunded item's quantity has usually been allocated again on another PO by `app:refund-purchase-orders`. After a rewind it counts again (`getQtyAddedToPurchaseOrders()` skips only cancelled and refunded items), so the line is on POs twice.

**4. The nightly refund skips rejected items on a mixed PO.**
- `app:refund-purchase-orders` handles POs whose overall status is REJECTED.
- A PO's status is its least advanced item. A rejected item next to an ACCEPTED one is never refunded or reallocated automatically.

**5. A partly allocated order is never picked up again by the schedule.**
- `app:build-purchase-orders` needs an order with no PO.
- If one line had no supplier with stock at the time, it waits for someone to click Allocate.

### To decide
- Should Allocate also move manually created PENDING PO items to PROCESSING when nothing is outstanding, or should a separate action do it?
- Should rewind leave REFUNDED and CANCELLED items alone?
- Should the schedule retry orders with outstanding quantity?

### Done when
Each case above has a test showing the intended behaviour. `Docs/04-sourcing-and-pricing.md` and `Docs/UserManual/09-order-items.md` / `10-purchase-orders.md` describe today's behaviour and need updating with the fix.

JNISleuth-MCP – Recover Stripped JNI Bindings and Ollvm Branches for Ghidra/Ida
Hi HN, I’m a security engineer focused on Android anti-malware and reverse engineering.
When reversing hardened Android apps or wild malware, one of the most tedious parts is crossing the Java-to-Native (JNI) boundary when `.so` binaries are stripped, methods are bound dynamically via `RegisterNatives` inside an OLLVM-flattened `JNI_OnLoad`, and `JNIEnv ` vtable calls decompile as raw pointer offsets like `(*(code *)( param_1 + 0x548))`.
I built JNISleuth-MCP to automate that workflow:
1. It parses multi-DEX APKs for `native` declarations and sweeps `.rodata` / `.data.rel.ro` (or section-header-stripped `PT_LOAD` segments) for `(char* name, char* sig, void* fnPtr)` triplets.
2. It statically resolves ARM64 OLLVM `CSEL` + `BR X8` indirect branches and `.rodata` jump tables in `JNI_OnLoad` (and can patch them in-place with direct `B.cond` / `B` instructions).
3. For runtime-packed samples that detect Frida, it includes a C++/NDK Dobby collector that hooks `RegisterNatives` mid-function.
4. It syncs the full 233-slot `JNIEnv*` vtable types and recovered C signatures into headless Ghidra and IDA Pro 9.0 (`idalib`/`idat64`), and exposes a model-agnostic MCP server + OpenAI/Gemini/Ollama tool schemas.
The repo includes a synthetic multi-DEX + stripped ARM64 `.so` crackme so you can test the entire pipeline in 30 seconds without needing a live malware sample. Would love feedback from anyone doing mobile RE or binary analysis!

## Problem

POST /api/reviews forwards req.body directly to createReview without schema validation. source_text:
HTTP Request node with pagination does not refresh credentials that use preAuthentication on 401
### Bug Description


The HTTP Request node does not renew an expired token for credentials that use `preAuthentication` (for example Microsoft Entra Service Principal) when pagination is enabled.

When the stored Microsoft Graph access token expires (every 60 to 90 minutes), Graph answers:

```
HTTP 401 {"error":{"code":"InvalidAuthenticationToken","message":"Invalid token lifetime."}}
```

n8n shows "Authorization failed - please check your credentials". "Retry On Fail" (3 tries, 5000 ms) does not help: all tries fail with the same error. The Microsoft Entra sign-in logs show no service principal sign-in during the failing executions, so n8n does not request a new token. The workflow works again only after another workflow uses the same credential without pagination, gets a 401, and renews the stored token.

Root cause (n8n 2.44.6, unchanged on master):

1. `requestWithAuthenticationPaginated` (`packages/core/src/execution-engine/node-execution-context/utils/request-helpers/pagination.ts`) sets `simple = false` and `resolveWithFullResponse = true` for each page.
2. Thus `requestWithAuthentication` (`.../request-helpers/authentication.ts`) resolves the 401 instead of throwing it. The `preAuthentication(credentialsExpired = true)` refresh and the resend exist only in its `catch` block, so they do not run.
3. `pagination.ts` then throws the 401 itself, outside the refresh path.
4. Each node retry reads the same expired token from the database.

`requestOAuth2` already handles a resolved 401 under `simple: false` (it throws it so that the token refresh runs). Credentials with `preAuthentication` do not get this handling. This affects all such credential types with HTTP Request pagination.

Related: #14426 (same symptom in the Microsoft Entra ID node, fixed in #30943 at node level).

### To Reproduce

1. Create a "Microsoft Entra Service Principal" credential for an app registration with the `Mail.Read` application permission.
2. Create a workflow: Schedule Trigger (every 10 minutes) → HTTP Request (typeVersion 4.2):
   - Authentication: Predefined Credential Type, Credential Type: Microsoft Entra Service Principal
   - `GET https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/users/<user>/mailFolders/inbox/messages`
   - Pagination: Mode "Response Contains Next URL", Next URL `{{ $response.body['@odata.nextLink'] }}`, Pagination Complete When "Other", Complete Expression `{{ !$response.body['@odata.nextLink'] }}`, Limit Pages Fetched: 10
   - Settings: Retry On Fail (3 tries, 5000 ms)
3. Use this credential in no other workflow.
4. Activate the workflow and wait until the first token expires (60 to 90 minutes).
5. All later executions fail with 401 "Invalid token lifetime". The Entra sign-in logs show no new service principal sign-in.

### Expected behavior

On a 401 for a page, n8n runs `preAuthentication` with `credentialsExpired = true`, stores the new token, and sends the page request again. This is the behavior without pagination and for OAuth2 credentials.

Show HN: VoidAccess – open-source dark web OSINT, from query to a graph
Hi HN! Im Katriel, and im a Security Researcher/Enthusiast and in the wave of AI, i wanted to build that next gen of security tooling that surpasses the current tools, and even the paid industries with an open source engine. I built MailAccess as well, which is going to be the best damn email osint tool out there, in another year. Very simple to run, you just run a few commands to install, and a couple to investigate. Then the engine takes over, and stops onyl when the job is done(or at a particular time limit, if set by the user). Do check it out, if that is something that interests you. Thanks to the community for giving it the love it has got till now.

### Bug Description

Structured content does not match the tool's output schema: data must NOT have additional properties

source_text:
Instance-level MCP: `search_workflow_executions` always fails output-schema validation after upgrading to 2.42.6
### Bug Description

After upgrading a self-hosted instance from 2.39.8 to 2.42.6, the instance-level MCP tool `search_workflow_executions` fails on every call from Claude (claude.ai custom connector) with:

```
Structured content does not match the tool's output schema: data must NOT have additional properties
```

It fails even with a filter that returns zero executions (a workflow with no executions), so the extra property seems to be on the root object of the structured response, not on individual execution rows. Other read tools work on the same connection: `search_workflows`, `get_workflow_details`, `get_workflow_execution` (metadata only), `search_nodes`, `get_node_types`. Refreshing the client's tool list does not help (same 13 tools, same schema). The same call worked on 2.39.8 with the same client and scopes (`workflow:read` + `execution:read`).

**Additional context**
Probably related to a change in the response shape (pagination or count fields) that was not reflected in the tool's `outputSchema` with `additionalProperties: false`. Clients that don't validate structured content may not notice.

### To Reproduce

1. Self-hosted n8n 2.42.6 (Docker, Postgres, `n8nio/runners` external), Instance-level MCP enabled, OAuth client with `workflow:read` + `execution:read`.
2. From an MCP client that validates `structuredContent` against `outputSchema` (Claude), call `search_workflow_executions` with any arguments, e.g. `{ "workflowId": "<any exposed workflow>", "limit": 5 }`.
3. The client rejects the result with the error above.

### Expected behavior

The tool's `structuredContent` matches its declared `outputSchema` (or the schema declares the new property), as in 2.39.8.

### Debug Info

- n8n version: 2.42.6 (self-hosted, Docker), upgraded from 2.39.8
- Database: Postgres 16
- Execution mode: regular (main) + external task runners
- MCP client: Claude (claude.ai custom connector), OAuth
- Hosting: Coolify

### Operating System

Ubuntu Linux 24.04 (Docker, Coolify)

### n8n Version

2.42.6

### Node.js Version

v26.7.0

### Database

PostgreSQL

### Execution mode

main (default)

### Hosting

self hosted

I think you're making the wrong takeaway here. LLMs aren't bad because of sycophancy tendencies. Any prediction at all is bad when it isn't based on r
I think you're making the wrong takeaway here. LLMs aren't bad because of sycophancy tendencies. Any prediction at all is bad when it isn't based on real data, whether or not it ends up being correct, whether or not it is made by an LLM, a human, or some other thing capable of spitting out a number. Analogize to basketball here. How confident are you that you can hit a free throw? If you ask someone who has played a thousand hours a year for the past ten years, has recorded their own statistics, and has averaged 70% success rate oer those past ten years, and they tell you they're 70% confident they can hit a free throw, that's a good prediction. If you ask me and I give you any prediction at all, I'm full of shit. I haven't played basketball or taken a free throw in 30 years. I can pull a number out of my ass, I can reason through it, I can do a Fermi, I can assume I'll be the average of all people who have ever tried and do my best to collect whatever data might exist on brand new players with no experience trying to take a free throw for the first time. I can narrow that to people my height, my age. Now we're getting better, but it's still not as good as having a real record of my actual past performance and basing a prediction off of that. This is just science. Hierarchy of evidence. Epistemology. Sometimes answering a question requires collecting data that doesn't exist yet and waiting a while, in the meantime admitting you don't have an answer. It was already sorely lacking in the world, but in this age of oracles, it's only getting worse.

T27G Epic: Trinity Game — guided onboarding quests, player progression and achievements
# T27G — Trinity Game / Quest System (Epic)

## Vision
Create the global game/quest layer for Trinity. The game teaches new participants how the product works through welcome screens and interactive gameplay, then tracks verified progression so each player can see their level, achievements and contribution history.

This is a system-level responsibility and should have a dedicated game agent/team, proposed code **T27G** (confirm naming against the existing 27-team registry before registering). T27G owns game design, onboarding quests, progression rules, badges/credentials and the integration contract between gameplay and real Trinity activity. It works under Queen's coordination and cooperates with T27U (University) rather than duplicating curriculum ownership.

## Core experience
1. A newcomer enters the Trinity world and starts a guided welcome quest.
2. Each quest step introduces one real product concept through the existing map/honeycomb and focused interactive scenes.
3. The player performs a meaningful action: explore a spec, complete a lesson, inspect a dependency, run a test, open or complete a task, or make a reviewed contribution.
4. The system records verified completion and advances quest/level progress.
5. The player sees a profile showing level, completed quests, earned badges and evidence-backed contributions.
6. Achievements can be shared through a stable public profile/achievement URL, with privacy controls.

## Agent boundary
- **T27G Game Agent:** game loop, onboarding, quest graph, progression/level rules, achievement criteria, badge/credential metadata, UX narrative and game telemetry.
- **T27U University Scientist:** canonical teaching content, course structure, learning objectives, theory modules and educational correctness.
- **Queen:** global coordination, assignment and cross-agent orchestration.
- Engineering agents: implement product capabilities and provide tests/evidence.
Avoid a second course engine, task tracker, profile store or orchestration framework. Reuse existing systems after auditing them.

## Progression and credentials
- A level must be derived from explicit, versioned rules and persisted quest events, not a decorative counter.
- A badge requires a defined criterion and evidence (completed lesson, passing test, reviewed contribution, etc.).
- Keep learning completion, contribution status, reputation and rewards as separate dimensions.
- Non-transferable on-chain credentials / soulbound tokens are a possible future delivery mechanism, not an assumed existing feature. First define a platform-neutral achievement schema and verify feasibility, privacy, wallet/account binding, revocation/correction, sybil resistance, cost and applicable chain standards. Do not promise token issuance or financial value before a tested implementation and approved policy.
- Avoid exposing private user activity. Public sharing must be opt-in and only expose approved evidence.

## Technical plan
### Phase 0 — audit
- Inspect existing game/Arena/map UI, welcome flow, course system, player identity/profile, task/test status, monitoring, agent registry and any token/credential code.
- Identify canonical event sources and persistence; document what exists vs missing.
- Reuse existing visual design and square-cell map; do not create a parallel game frontend.

### Phase 1 — vertical slice
- One first-time-user onboarding quest with 5–7 short steps.
- At least one step links to a real honeycomb cell/spec and one step to a T27U course/lesson.
- At least one practical step is verified against a real task/test/event rather than self-reported click completion.
- Persist quest progress and derive a level from explicit rules.
- Award one test badge with criterion, timestamp/version and evidence reference.
- Display a progress view and a shareable achievement page, with privacy-safe defaults.
- Include skip/resume/replay paths, accessibility, mobile layout and reduced-motion support.

### Phase 2 — extensible game system
- Data-driven quest definitions and prerequisites.
- Reusable quest-step types and validation handlers.
- Versioned levels/badge rules and migration strategy.
- Admin/agent-authoring workflow with review and safe publication.
- Optional credential adapter after platform-neutral badge model is validated.

## Acceptance criteria
- New participant can complete onboarding without prior knowledge and understand the map, specs, agents and how to make a useful contribution.
- Quest completion and level are reproducible from persisted events and documented rules.
- At least one achievement is awarded only after evidence validation.
- T27G and T27U responsibilities are clear and integrated without duplicate systems.
- Existing map/course/task systems are reused; no parallel dashboard or fake progress.
- Security/privacy review covers shared profiles, forged events, replay, identity binding and any future token mechanism.
- Tests, telemetry, known limitations and a next-phase roadmap are included.

## Explicit non-goals for MVP
- No token price, financial reward or GPU payout promises.
- No requirement to deploy a blockchain credential in the first slice.
- No arbitrary scripts embedded in social posts; shared links open a safe Trinity-hosted quest.
- No redesign of the existing honeycomb map.

## Deliverables
1. Architecture audit and component reuse map.
2. T27G agent/team definition using the actual registry convention.
3. Quest schema, progression rules and badge evidence model.
4. Working onboarding vertical slice and tests.
5. Documented credential adapter proposal, including trade-offs and decision gate.

source_text:
Show HN: Hindsight – Lightweight, elegant, open-source tracker for Windows/macOS
Hi HN, I’m building Hindsight, a free, open-source activity tracker for Windows and macOS. I know there are plenty of time trackers. I wanted something that combined automatic tracking, detailed charts, and cross-device sync in a lightweight app with an interface I enjoyed using. I couldn’t find a free option that fit, so I started building my own. Hindsight records active apps and window titles while it’s running, without requiring you to start and stop timers. You can explore your activity through daily, weekly, and monthly charts, drill down into individual apps and window titles, and use a yearly heatmap to spot patterns. Categories are customizable. There’s also an optional screenshot and OCR feature for finding something you previously saw on screen. Both are off by default. When enabled, you can search recognized text and jump back to the corresponding screenshot. The AI features can generate daily summaries or answer questions about your activity, with links back to the underlying records so you can check the answers. You can use a local model or connect a cloud API; third-party API fees may apply. Optional sync through Google Drive or WebDAV lets you view activity from Windows and Mac devices separately or together. I’ve also recently added plugin support so other developers can extend the app. I’d appreciate feedback, particularly on how you’d want to explore your activity history. What would make this useful to you beyond simply showing how many hours you spent in each app? Happy to answer questions about how it works.

source_text:
Vienna, a year ago.  A quiet, dark little bar, Schwartze Flamingo.  A friend and I are sitting there on a Thursday evening, kinda bored.  It’s the sor
Vienna, a year ago.  A quiet, dark little bar, Schwartze Flamingo.  A friend and I are sitting there on a Thursday evening, kinda bored.  It’s the sort of place that just feels like it’s missing something.  Plenty of space for it, whatever it is.  Just, missing. I look up from my beer, which I kinda don’t want, and say to my friend, “there’s gotta be something better to do than sit here getting drunk..”, and as I say it, I look over his shoulder, my eye caught by the glint of some shiny thing.  Looking closer, it’s a sticker on the divider of our booth, ‘Pinball Crew Vienna’ .. “like .. we could find and then play pinball, for instance!”, I exclaim, kind of half assed. My friend looks over his shoulder too, and takes a picture of the sticker, and goes quiet for a moment while he looks things up .. “well, there’s a tournament tomorrow, and its in our neighborhood .. I’ve never played pinball, whats it like?” What?!! Where?! “In the IKEA building at the Westbahnhof”.   A building I had, to that point kind of despised, because I loathe IKEA in general. Nevertheless, the next weekend, we put away our aversions to global particle board distribution, and make our way to the Westbahnhof .. Jo+Joes, a hostel I had no idea existed, occupies the 5th floor.  The elevator opens, and it is like the pearly gates spreading wide, disco balls for miles to see, a joyous bright and pastel atmosphere, people laughing everywhere, smiles from wall to wall .. and oh, so many pinball machines! “VIENNA IS LIT!”, scream the posters, and the immediately recognizable sound of flipping spinners, drop target resets, inevitable drain lanes and bumpers galore, greet us. I immediately sign up for the tournament.  I haven’t played pinball properly - for fun or for competition - in 40 some odd years.  I’d grown up on a beach esplanade in Australia, my Dad’s burger shop, where I’d witnessed the many much loved pinball machines of my distant memories, slowly at first, and then suddenly like a fever, be replaced with Breakout and Space Invaders, the first ‘real computers’ I’d ever seen as a small kid. All the memories come back.  The love I had for that one drop target that’d get a free game, the shock of the bump targets, perfectly aligned, sending another coin into the slot.  The delightful whiff of solenoids and window cleaner.  The internal wiring I felt in myself, changing, adjusting to new things learned.  That old familiar hacker vibe, at its root, analog and perfectly shaped. So, I played for 6 hours straight, just blistering everything I could extend .. and I came 63 out of 65 competitors, and it was a BLAST! Just walking past the 30 or so machines, crammed into this crazy hostel I’d not known even existed due to my prejudices and bigotries, replaced now with curiosity and a kind of relief .. all the good times came flooding back - and now, as a seasoned systems engineer in his 50’s, it was just the right time, too.  Newly divorced, trying to find myself a bit, in a city that will eat you alive slowly, this was the perfect new (old) hobby for these weary bones. I play every week.  I joined a pinball club, started my own team, made us t-shirts.  The weekly journey to FlipperAsyl (perfectly named) injects life and joy and vigor into things again. The IKEA building is our meeting point now, they have two tables permanently installed .. Wrestlemania and Avengers.  We only play Avengers, our little group have a competitive edge, and every month one of us takes the throne, having learned some new tricks or two. Eventually we connect with the other folks in our neighborhood .. slowly all our high scores are erased by one FLO, who we track down and invite and challenge, on the regular. Pinball is a quantum machine for calculating fun  and  disappointment, but mostly fun. It is powered by human soul. Play it with your friends, teach each other things as you learn them, get to know the table and get to know yourselves. Each table has lessons to learn, the generations themselves visible in every machine.  The soul of thousands of fun-seekers can be felt, if you pay attention to the quirks and rhythms.  The spirit in the machine is really there, I promise.  You can feel it. Had Barracora at home for a few months, she felt positively possessed, and for many weeks, was our little shrine. Got Swords of Fury at home, now. My pinball club leases tables to trusted members - a solution to the GAS that afflicts the pinball crew. (Gear Acquisition Syndrome - i.e. too many tables not enough room) There’s another twist.  Pinball is a male-dominated sport. Our little team of discarded men, new fathers, old fathers, some of us recovering addicts, some just in it for fun - we have bonded over the tricks and details, this past year.  It has been a truly unifying experience for our little club of men. But FlipperAsyl has ladies nights too - necessary because we men do tend to dominate - and that is also fun to observe at a distance. There is cross-pollination too of course - I regularly learn major things from some of the nice regular ladies in the Asyl. It has been soothing and healing. We’ve already mapped out all the pinball machines we can find in the city, before one of us discovered the pinball map .. so now there’s a day trip planned, to the Pinball Museum Budapest, and our little merry crew of pinball misfits will make that train journey some day soon.  It’s gonna be GREAT. So .. yeah .. “VIENNA IS LIT!”, is happening again this year, in case any HN’ers are in town and want another GREAT hobby to apply themselves to .. hey, if you’re out of town, maybe get yourself a plane ticket, get yourself booked into JO+JOES, and get ready for 2 days of PURE FUN.  https://events.eventjet.at/e/vienna-is-lit-wiens-groesstes-f...  See you there!

EU supplier/shipping-origin data source for BOM (free, maintained)
Useful project — quantity mapping is exactly the hard part of PrintNC builds.

One data gap for EU users: the same part list has very different landed cost depending on shipping origin. US-direct orders end up +40–50% after customs/VAT handling, while the same parts from EU warehouses (PL/DE/CZ/ES) arrive in 3–10 days with zero customs. There are also a few recurring part-spec traps (1605 vs 1610 ballscrew ends, anti-backlash nut handedness, rail length vs travel) that a generator could validate.

I maintain a free, per-build BOM→EU-supplier mapping here (quantities, supplier paths, ordering traps):

Looking for AI Chatbot That Can Use External Knowledge Base (TXT/CSV) for Support & Product Info
Hi all, 
 I’m looking for a Shopify-compatible AI chatbot that can respond to customer questions using  a structured knowledge base  — like a TXT or CSV file — rather than relying only on what’s in Shopify’s product listings. 
 Many of my product options and configurations are managed through a  third-party product options app , so I can’t rely on Shopify’s native catalog alone. I need a bot that can: 
 
 Import and reference external data (ideally via TXT or CSV) 
 Respond  only using the content I provide , without making things up or rewording 
 Follow a consistent format with specific titles and URLs (not summaries or paraphrases) 
 Be powered by something like ChatGPT, so it can follow clear instructions 
 Integrate with my Shopify storefront 
 
 Here’s the thing — I’ve already been able to get this working exactly how I want using ChatGPT directly , but none of the Shopify app store bots I’ve tried so far come close to that level of control or reliability. They often lack file upload support, or they try to guess and summarize — which just doesn’t work for what I need. 
 If anyone out there has found a solution — app, workaround, or even a custom integration — that can do this kind of knowledge-based chatbot well inside Shopify, I’d love to hear about it. 
 Thanks in advance!

Desarrollador de Automatizaciones e IA | n8n, WhatsApp, Agentes IA, APIs y Supabase | Busco proyectos/equipo
¡Hola a todos! Soy Milton, desarrollador de Argentina, y actualmente estoy buscando proyectos freelance, colaboraciones o la posibilidad de sumarme a un equipo que trabaje con IA y automatización. 
 Durante los últimos años estuve trabajando en desarrollo de software y actualmente estoy especializado en crear  agentes de IA y sistemas de automatización con n8n aplicados a negocios reales . 
 Algunas de las soluciones que desarrollé: 
 
 Agentes de IA integrados con  WhatsApp Business . 
 Captura, filtrado y calificación automática de leads. 
 Integraciones mediante  APIs REST, webhooks y JSON . 
 Automatizaciones con  n8n + Supabase/PostgreSQL . 
 Agentes capaces de ejecutar herramientas y acciones dentro de otros sistemas. 
 Derivación automática a una persona cuando la conversación lo requiere. 
 Sistemas de  reserva, consulta de disponibilidad, reprogramación y cancelación de turnos . 
 Flujos  Meta Ads → WhatsApp → Agente IA → Base de datos/CRM → Dashboard . 
 Notificaciones y seguimientos automáticos. 
 Dashboards personalizados para administrar conversaciones, clientes y leads. 
 
 Uno de mis principales proyectos fue el desarrollo de un sistema para  agencias de autos , donde las consultas provenientes de campañas publicitarias son atendidas automáticamente por un agente de IA en WhatsApp. 
 El agente conversa con el potencial cliente, recopila y valida información, consulta herramientas, registra los datos en Supabase, actualiza un dashboard propio y deriva la conversación al equipo comercial cuando corresponde. 
 También estoy trabajando en sistemas más complejos de  orquestación de agentes y turnos , combinando IA con lógica de negocio determinística para conseguir automatizaciones más confiables y mantenibles. 
 Mi stack principal: 
  n8n · JavaScript/TypeScript · React · Supabase · PostgreSQL · REST APIs · Webhooks · WhatsApp Business · OpenAI/Gemini/LLMs · Meta  
 Actualmente me interesa especialmente colaborar con  agencias de automatización, equipos que desarrollen agentes de IA, productos SaaS o empresas que necesiten implementar este tipo de sistemas . 
 Estoy en Argentina (UTC-3) y tengo disponibilidad para trabajar de manera remota, tanto en  proyectos freelance como colaboraciones a largo plazo o una posición dentro de un equipo . 
 Puedo compartir por privado capturas, workflows, arquitectura y demos de los sistemas que desarrollé. 
  LinkedIn:   linkedin.com/in/miltonpinzone/  
 GitHub:   milton1471 (Milton Pinzone) · GitHub  
 Si alguien está buscando un perfil técnico para desarrollar este tipo de soluciones, puede escribirme por DM. 
 ¡Gracias!

Show HN: Standard Topic – An AI and RSS-powered news and resource platform
Hi HN, I'm John, a knowledge management and AI enablement professional. I created Standard Topic, an AI and RSS-powered news and resource platform, with assistance from Claude Code. Standard Topic uses AI integrations and RSS feeds to curate news and resources across relevant topics and presents these in the form of top stories, trending items, and a curated prompt library to easily gather further context on a given topic (examples of topics being World News, Politics, Business, Technology, Sports, Science, Health and more.) On topic hubs, you can find a regularly updated at-a-glance AI briefings providing relevant updates, top stories with AI insights and cited sources, and additional recent news coverage. A governance system is in place with AI assisting in ranking stories, retiring items from the top stories section, determining which additional news is displayed, and more. An AI-generated briefing podcast, in the format of a radio news program, releases each morning and evening (5 AM and 5 PM ET), covering the latest global news. While in the past I've released apps and websites that felt duct-taped together and which I stopped using after some time, with this one I've actually found myself using it more than Twitter/X and other daily news briefing platforms, while also leading me to more frequently engage directly with publishing platforms cited on Standard Topic. My recent work in AI has been around finding practical uses in the content and knowledge management areas for integrating the technology, and Standard Topic has developed into what I see as a product that uses structured outputs and automated insights to deliver consistent and trustworthy, cited content while maintaining transparency about being primarily powered by artificial intelligence. There's still some kinks to work out in terms of automated workflows, design aspects and more. Let me know what you think!
