Halal Certification in Papua New Guinea
Halal Certification in Papua New Guinea: Expanding Food Business Opportunities
Introduction
Food manufacturers, exporters, restaurants, hospitality providers, and distributors must increasingly demonstrate that their products meet specific customer and market requirements. For businesses serving Muslim consumers or working with international food supply chains, Halal compliance can be an important part of product acceptance and business development.
[Halal Certification in Papua New Guinea](https://certvalue.com/halal-certification-in-papua-new-guinea/) helps eligible businesses demonstrate that their products, ingredients, handling practices, and relevant production processes comply with the requirements of the applicable Halal certification programme. CertValue supports organizations with compliance preparation, documentation, and certification coordination.
What Is Halal Certification?
Halal refers to products and practices permitted under Islamic dietary principles. Certification generally involves assessing relevant ingredients, sourcing arrangements, production processes, hygiene practices, storage, handling, and measures to prevent contamination with prohibited substances.
The exact requirements depend on the product category and the certification body. Businesses should select a certification provider whose recognition and scope meet their intended customers' and export markets' requirements.
Key Business Benefits
Halal certification can help organizations strengthen their market position in several ways:
Market development: Demonstrating Halal compliance can help businesses approach eligible buyers and distributors serving Muslim consumers.
Customer confidence: Documented processes provide greater transparency about ingredients and production controls.
Supply-chain assurance: Ingredient traceability and supplier evaluation can improve oversight.
Process consistency: Defined handling and segregation procedures can reduce the risk of cross-contamination.
Brand credibility: Appropriate certification can support marketing and commercial discussions where Halal assurance is required.
Certification does not automatically guarantee acceptance in every country or market, so recognition requirements should be checked before making export commitments.
Industries That Can Benefit
Halal certification may be relevant to food processors, meat and poultry businesses, seafood suppliers, beverage manufacturers, ingredient producers, restaurants, catering companies, and food distributors.
For example, a food manufacturer supplying wholesale customers can review ingredient sources, production records, cleaning procedures, storage arrangements, and product labelling. A hospitality business can establish suitable purchasing and food-handling procedures for the products covered by its certification.
Non-food products and services may also fall within particular Halal certification programmes, depending on their scope.
Steps to Prepare for Certification
Businesses can follow a structured process:
Define the scope: Identify the products, facilities, and activities for which Halal certification is required.
Review ingredients: Check raw materials, additives, processing aids, and supplier documentation.
Assess production processes: Review equipment, cleaning, storage, handling, and segregation arrangements.
Prepare documentation: Maintain ingredient lists, supplier records, procedures, and traceability information.
Train employees: Explain relevant handling requirements and responsibilities.
Complete the assessment: Submit the application and undergo the required review or audit.
Maintain compliance: Follow surveillance, renewal, and change-notification requirements where applicable.
How CertValue Supports Your Business
CertValue assists businesses with gap assessments, documentation preparation, implementation guidance, and coordination of certification requirements. This support helps organizations organize evidence and prepare for assessment by an appropriate Halal certification body.
Conclusion
[Halal Certification in Papua New Guinea](https://certvalue.com/halal-certification-in-papua-new-guinea/) can help eligible businesses demonstrate compliance with relevant Halal requirements and develop stronger relationships with customers, distributors, and supply-chain partners.

I find this guy kinda annoying.  I mean, yeah...seems like he did some networking back in the day, but everything he posts is  just  enough off (or ia
I find this guy kinda annoying.  I mean, yeah...seems like he did some networking back in the day, but everything he posts is  just  enough off (or ia Google-correct, not Been-There-correct) that I can't quite take him seriously.  The main reason Ethernet won the war was because it was cheaper.  He should have stopped there.  That was it.  And because it was cheaper, less complicated to build the chips, 'good enough' networking, a bunch of folks jumped on the bandwagon.  And here we are.  If you had a 16 megabit network and brought up a system at 4 megabits, it took down the whole network.  Well, yes,  everyone  who has ever mentioned TR tells some variation of this.  And if you left the terminator off of the coax ethernet, you brought the whole network down.  But TR got smart MAUs and ethernet got UTP hubs around the same time and problem solved. And hubs were a lot cheaper than smart MAUs.  Sooo...  Ethernet was junk if you went with the cheapest options all around, but you could make it acceptable if you invested some of the savings in improved technology.  Just like TR.  If you were deploying dirt cheap 8228s after 1990 or so, your network still sucked.  You didn't do that.  But the other reason Ethernet won was because of scale.  Yes, there was a thing called 100Mb Token Ring.  Someone might have even shipped some number of them.  I never saw one in the wild, and I don't know anyone who claimed they had who didn't work for IBM or Madge (which, btw, wasn't an 'obscure' network company at the time and made more than just TR cards). That's because basically everyone who did Token Ring (IBM most of all) had decided that you wanted to scale TR you were going to ATM (for a bunch of mostly political and marketing reasons).  Which, unlike TR, was  in reality  a very bad idea, but that's another story. I've never even heard anyone even suggest 128Mb Token Ring, and I suspect someones LLM is hallucinating.  There  was  a gigabit Token Ring standard (IEEE 802.5v), but I feel pretty confident saying noone ever shipped it.  Like I said...ATM was gonna be the future.  Ethernet used a 15-pin connector that looks quite a bit like a PC joystick connector. Token Ring used a 9-pin connector that looks like a 9-pin video connector or an Atari style joystick plug.  Ok...I'll just be snarky and point out there are ethernet cards that use a 9-pin D-sub connector to reuse a TR wiring physical plant.  I have several.  Coax connectors for Token Ring did exist  Citation needed.  I've seen coax for 802. 4  industrial networking stuff, which is not TR.  I'm betting more hallucinations.  ARCNET was another competitor from the same timeframe. It, too, was a contender for a while because it was backed by Datapoint, a pioneer in office automation using small computers.  Arcnet was a contender because it was even cheaper than ethernet and it was (and still is) widely used in industrial environments.  And some popular early PC file sharing systems (e.g. LANTastic) would use Arcnet.

Spec: Account registration by invitation (Thailand)
Design for #6. Local source: `docs/specs/0004-account-registration/index.md`.

Brief traceability:
- Requirement 1.1: "The system shall allow store staff to register their accounts."
- Requirement 1.2: "The system shall allow store managers to register their accounts."

# 0004. Account registration by invitation

**Date**: 2026-11-07
**Status**: Proposed

## Summary

Staff and managers register through an invitation issued by a local operator. The invitation fixes their employee code, role, and branch; the recipient supplies their name, Thai mobile number, and password. Registration creates an account without a session, with phone ownership checked by OTP at first sign in in issue #7. This slice also aligns the shop timezone and demo data with Thailand.

## Requirements

**User stories**:

- As an operator, I want to invite a staff member or manager to a specific branch without needing an existing signed in account.
- As an invited employee, I want to create my account with my own Thai mobile number and password.
- As a manager, I want invitation reuse and duplicate phone numbers to be refused so accounts keep their intended identity and access.

**Acceptance criteria**:

- **AC-1**: The operator command issues an invitation for either `STAFF` or `MANAGER`, an existing active branch, and an assigned employee code. It prints the registration URL once, stores only a token hash, and sets expiry to 48 hours after creation. Invalid roles, inactive or unknown branches, and employee codes already attached to an account fail without creating an invitation.
- **AC-2**: Issuing another invitation for the same employee code revokes the previous outstanding invitation atomically. The operator can revoke an unused invitation explicitly. Expired, revoked, consumed, and unknown invitations cannot register an account; expiry is checked again after any lock wait or password hashing.
- **AC-3**: Opening a valid invitation at `/register` loads its real branch name, employee code, role, and expiry from the API. Missing or unavailable invitations show a useful recovery message and no enabled registration form. Preview does not consume an invitation or disclose account credentials.
- **AC-4**: Submitting a valid invitation, full name, Thai mobile number, and password creates exactly one `staff_account` with the invitation's role, branch, and employee code, `email = NULL`, and an Argon2id password hash. The entered password verifies against the stored hash and a different password does not.
- **AC-5**: Domestic and international forms of the same Thai mobile number normalize to one `+66…` value. Invalid input returns field errors. A duplicate normalized phone, including one belonging to an inactive account, returns a clear conflict and creates no account. This remains true for simultaneous submissions with different invitations.
- **AC-6**: Account insertion, invitation consumption, and the successful registration audit event commit together. Simultaneous use of one invitation produces at most one account. Failure rolls back all three effects. Retrying after an uncertain network outcome cannot create a second account or change the original password.
- **AC-7**: Registration issues no session cookie and writes no `staff_session` or `otp_challenge`. Client supplied role, branch, employee code, or active status cannot change the invitation's grant. No sign in or OTP delivery endpoint ships in this slice.
- **AC-8**: Both public registration endpoints enforce the request limit described below before database access. Password hashing has a fixed concurrency bound. Responses use the shared HTTP envelopes; logs contain neither passwords, raw tokens, phone numbers, full names, nor request bodies. Invitation history and the registration event remain available for audit.
- **AC-9**: The registration screen reuses the existing design tokens and form parts, works at phone, tablet, and desktop widths, and supports keyboard use. Loading, invalid invitation, field error, duplicate phone, throttling, network uncertainty, and success states are accessible. Submit is disabled while pending, and success clearly states that the account exists but the person is not signed in.
- **AC-10**: The shop uses `Asia/Bangkok`; demo branches, staff, members, suppliers, and descriptive seed copy use Thailand context. Sample money is consistently THB and the seed's derived totals remain consistent. The D15 documentation is explicitly revised. No existing stored phone number, monetary value, or applied migration is silently rewritten.
- **AC-11**: The schema change applies to an existing database and a fresh database through the normal migration runner. The baseline checksum remains unchanged. The temporary foundation echo endpoint is removed when these real domain endpoints are wired. The root tests, typecheck, lint, and format check pass; runtime verification proves the screen, API response, and stored result for both roles.

## Decision

**Chosen option**: Invitations issued by a local operator, using the existing account table and application stack.

Use Hono and Zod for the API, Bun SQL repositories for persistence, Bun's asynchronous Argon2id functions for passwords, and the existing Next.js shell for `/register`. Add one invitation table and one registration audit event type. No new service or package is required.

**Confirmed business rules**: Both roles require an invitation. The operator chooses role, branch, and employee code. The invitation is not bound to a phone number. It expires after 48 hours, and reissuing it revokes the previous link. Email is omitted. Thai phone ownership is checked at first sign in, in issue #7.

**Scope boundary**: Issue #6's phrase “the new account can sign in with its password” means the stored credentials are ready for issue #7. Here, prove password verification against the stored hash. Actual sign in requires password plus OTP and remains issue #7. A password alone never creates a session.

## Feature design

### Data model

Add `database/migrations/0002_staff_invitations.sql`. Do not edit `0001_baseline.sql`.

| Entity | Fields and relationships | Constraints |
|---|---|---|
| `branch` | Existing table, one branch to many accounts and invitations | Referenced branch must be active at invitation creation and redemption |
| `staff_account` | Existing columns and constraints. UUID `id` generated by PostgreSQL. `full_name`, canonical `phone`, and `password_hash` supplied by registration; `branch_id`, `employee_code`, and `role` copied from invitation; `email = NULL`; `is_active = true`; `created_at` from database | Existing global unique phone and employee code apply to active and inactive accounts alike |
| `staff_invitation` | UUID `id` with `gen_random_uuid()` default; required `branch_id` FK to `branch`; required text `employee_code`; required `role staff_role`; required unique text `token_hash`; required `created_at` and `expires_at` as `timestamptz`; nullable `revoked_at`, `consumed_at` as `timestamptz`; nullable unique UUID `consumed_by` FK to `staff_account` | Hash is 64 lowercase hexadecimal characters. `expires_at > created_at`. Consumption time and account reference are either both null or both present. Revoked and consumed cannot both be present. Terminal timestamps cannot precede creation. A partial unique index on employee code where `consumed_at IS NULL AND revoked_at IS NULL` permits only one outstanding invitation, including an expired one until reissue revokes it. Index `branch_id` |
| `auth_event` | Existing table; append `REGISTERED` to `auth_event_type`. Successful creation inserts `staff_id`, `type = REGISTERED`, `success = true`, peer IP when available, and database creation time | Event and account commit in the same transaction. The new enum value is first used after the migration commits |

Invitation grants are immutable. Reissue creates a new row and retains the revoked row. No row is hard deleted. One consumed invitation references one created account. The invitation's retained timestamps record issuance, revocation, and consumption; the `REGISTERED` event records the account creation.

`is_active = true` means the account may attempt sign in. It does not mean its phone has been verified or that a session exists. This feature adds no phone verification flag, account approval state, or second account table.

### Invitation lifecycle and transactions

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Available: Operator issues invitation
    Available --> Consumed: Account and audit event commit
    Available --> Revoked: Operator revokes or reissues
    Available --> Expired: Database clock reaches expiry
    Expired --> Revoked: Operator revokes or reissues
```

`Expired` is derived from the timestamp, so no timer or stored status is needed. An invitation is usable only when it is unconsumed, unrevoked, not expired, and its branch is active. Preview is advisory; redemption repeats the checks inside its transaction.

All issue, revoke, and redeem transactions serialize operations for an employee code using `pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended('staff-registration:' || employee_code, 0))`. This is a PostgreSQL transaction lock, released on commit or rollback. Bind the employee code through the existing tagged SQL seam. Lock order is employee code, invitation row, then branch row. Lock existing invitation rows with `FOR UPDATE`; issuance and redemption also lock the branch with `FOR SHARE` to prevent deactivation during the operation. Revocation needs no branch lock. Database unique constraints remain the final protection for phone and employee code.

**Issue**: Validate arguments and resolve the branch code. Generate the token in memory. In one transaction take the employee lock, reject an existing account with that employee code, lock any outstanding invitation for the code, then lock and recheck the branch. Revoke the outstanding invitation and insert the replacement. Take the new creation time once from the database and set expiry to that time plus 48 hours. Print the URL only after commit. If the commit outcome is uncertain, report uncertainty and print no URL; running issue again safely revokes any committed but undisclosed invitation.

**Revoke**: Resolve the invitation ID to its immutable employee code, take the employee lock, and lock the invitation row. Mark an unused invitation revoked. Already revoked is a successful no change result. A consumed invitation returns a conflict and does not deactivate the created account. An unknown ID is an error. Revocation does not require an active branch.

**Register**:

1. Apply request limits and validate the body. Hash the supplied token and do a cheap eligibility read before expensive password hashing.
2. Acquire a password hashing slot, hash the password asynchronously, and release the slot in `finally`. Hash outside the database transaction.
3. Begin the repository transaction, take the employee lock, lock the invitation row, and lock the branch. Recheck the grant and expiry using `clock_timestamp()` after lock acquisition, so an expired link cannot pass using a stale transaction start time.
4. Insert the account using `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING ...`. If no row is inserted, distinguish an existing canonical phone from another account conflict using a fresh query. Return the domain conflict without consuming the invitation. Do not inspect or expose raw database error details.
5. Mark the invitation consumed with the inserted account ID and insert the `REGISTERED` event. Commit before returning success.

Use the existing transaction retry policy for serialization failures and deadlocks. Reuse the already computed password hash within such a retry. Do not automatically retry an uncertain commit or perform external effects inside the callback.

### Validation

| Value | Rule |
|---|---|
| Invitation token | Exactly 43 URL safe base64 characters from 32 cryptographically random bytes, without padding. No trimming or alternate encodings |
| Employee code | Operator input, trim and uppercase; 3 to 32 ASCII characters matching `[A-Z0-9][A-Z0-9-]{2,31}`. No case conversion of existing database records |
| Branch code | Operator input, trim and uppercase, then exact lookup of `branch.code` |
| Role | Exactly `STAFF` or `MANAGER` |
| Full name | Trim outer whitespace, normalize to NFC, then 1 to 100 Unicode code points. Reject control characters. Allow Thai and other scripts, spaces, punctuation, and single word names |
| Phone | Input string up to 40 characters. Trim, remove ASCII spaces, hyphens, and parentheses, then accept `0[689][0-9]{8}` or `\+66[689][0-9]{8}`. Replace the domestic leading zero with `+66`. Reject other characters, extensions, foreign country codes, and `+660…`. Do not normalize Thai numeral glyphs silently |
| Password | 15 to 128 Unicode code points. Accept spaces and Unicode; no composition rules, trimming, normalization, or truncation. Reject invalid Unicode sequences. The UI confirms the password locally; confirmation is not stored or sent |

The phone rule is a format policy for the supported Thai mobile forms, not proof that a number is allocated, reachable, SMS capable, or owned by the recipient. Issue #7 establishes possession through OTP. The backend is authoritative; browser validation provides early feedback. `0812345678`, `081-234-5678`, and `+66 81 234 5678` all become `+66812345678`.

Use `Bun.password.hash(password, { algorithm: "argon2id", memoryCost: 65536, timeCost: 3 })` and `Bun.password.verify`. These are application policy values: 64 MiB and three passes per hash. Store the encoded hash returned by Bun, including its salt and parameters.

Set `Cache-Control: no-store` on both endpoints, including errors.

Add these entries to the shared error catalog:

| Code | HTTP | Message and use |
|---|---|---|
| `INVITATION_UNAVAILABLE` | 400 | `This invitation is unavailable. Ask the operator for a new invitation.` Used uniformly for unknown, expired, revoked, consumed, or inactive branch grants |

### Security and operational limits

The invitation is a bearer capability: anyone possessing it may claim its role and branch. This is the user's chosen policy. The operator must deliver it privately; a fixed phone binding and automatic delivery are outside this slice. Store SHA256 of the exact UTF-8 token string as lowercase hex. A slow password hash is unnecessary for a random 256 bit invitation token.

Both registration endpoints share an in memory fixed window limit of 20 requests per 60 seconds per connection peer IP, applied after CORS/body limits and before body parsing or database access. Do not trust forwarded IP headers. `server.ts` obtains the peer address from `server.requestIP(request)` and passes it to Hono through typed bindings; unavailable addresses share an `unknown` bucket. Tests inject the binding explicitly. Expire buckets lazily, cap the map at 10,000 active keys, and reject new keys with 429 when full rather than evicting active counters. Preflight does not consume the budget. Expose `Retry-After` to the allowed client origin.

Allow at most two password hashes concurrently per process, with no unbounded waiting queue. If both slots are occupied, return 429 with `Retry-After: 1`. Both limits are constants with injectable clocks or adapters for tests, not new environment settings. Counters reset on process restart and are not shared across replicas. This slice targets the current single server process; a shared limiter is a later deployment decision.

Use a generated request UUID and structured registration outcome logs with only the request ID, operation, outcome, status, and nonsecret invitation or account IDs when known. Never log body content, URL fragments, token hashes, phone numbers, names, passwords, or raw database errors. CLI stdout is the one intentional disclosure of a raw invitation URL. Failed requests cannot write misleading success audit events.

Use HTTPS outside localhost. This course slice uses synthetic demonstration records; it does not claim legal compliance or establish a personal data retention policy for a real deployment.

## Consequences

**Positive**:

- Registration works before sign in exists, including the first manager account.
- Roles and branches are granted by an operator, and database transactions protect invitation consumption and account uniqueness.
- Existing runtime, HTTP, data, and UI foundations carry the feature without another provider.

**Negative / tradeoffs**:

- An operator must create and privately deliver each link. A recipient can forward it because it is not bound to a phone.
- A mistyped phone can be stored before OTP proves ownership. Account correction and recovery require a later design; registration cannot overwrite an existing account.
- An uncertain response may require operator help. The design guarantees at most one account, but does not replay a successful receipt after the token is consumed.
- Rate limits are local to one server process. Distributed deployment will need a shared policy and trusted proxy configuration.
- Thailand fixture work extends beyond authentication because country context is shared across the demo.

**Neutral**:

- One new table brings the domain table count to 26; existing lifecycle assertions must reflect that.
- D15 changes explicitly. Other schema decisions and the baseline migration stay intact.

# Account registration rationale

## Context

Issue #6 covers requirements 1.1 and 1.2, staff and manager registration. The schema already has a shared account table with a required branch, globally unique phone and employee code, password hash, and role. The HTTP seam, Bun SQL repository layer, and signed out UI foundation are built. Sign in and OTP remain issue #7.

Public role selection would give anyone a path to manager privileges once sign in lands. Conversely, requiring a signed in manager to create every invitation would prevent bootstrapping the first manager and make registration depend on its own downstream sign in feature. The team needs a working database, API, and screen slice before later management screens.

The user chose invitations for both roles, issuance through a local operator command, an operator assigned employee code, no phone binding, no email field, a 48 hour lifetime, and revocation on reissue. Phone ownership is proved at first sign in. The user then requested Thailand context throughout, including phone numbers, timezone, and demo records. That explicitly replaces the prior Vietnam context and D15 timezone.

## Options considered

### Option 1: Public registration with role and branch selection

This needs the least code and matches a simple course demonstration form.

**Pros**: Immediate registration with no invitation workflow or operator step.

**Cons**: Anyone can claim manager access. Adding approval later changes account activation and authorization semantics.

### Option 2: Operator issued invitations

A trusted local command creates a single use grant for an employee code, role, and branch. The recipient completes their own account through the web page.

**Pros**: Works for the first manager, enforces grant authority before accounts exist, and fits the current database and application stack.

**Cons**: The operator delivers links manually, and a link may be forwarded. The team owns the small invitation lifecycle and its concurrency tests.

### Option 3: Invitations managed by signed in managers

A manager screen controls invitations with explicit permission rules and an actor identity from the session.

**Pros**: Better daily operation and attribution when authentication already exists.

**Cons**: Requires sign in, OTP, and a bootstrap mechanism before this slice can work. It also requires a policy for which managers can grant manager roles.

## Rationale

Choose option 2. It solves the authority and bootstrap problems together while keeping the sale flow moving. Option 3 is the natural later extension. The operator command is a trusted maintenance boundary, so there is no public route that can grant roles.

Reuse Bun's password functions and the existing account schema. Introducing another identity provider would add an account mapping and operational dependency without replacing the agreed OTP and session requirements in this slice. Keep registration separate from session establishment and prove its stored credential contract with real hash verification. This is a deliberate use of the existing design, not a new session protocol.

Use a random token with only its hash stored, a URL fragment for delivery, and JSON bodies for API requests. A query parameter would be simpler but would expose the token to normal URL logging. Removing the fragment after reading it reduces browser history exposure at the cost of requiring the original link after a refresh.

Use a transaction for account creation, invitation consumption, and the registration audit event. An employee code lock also serializes reissue against redemption. Database uniqueness independently protects duplicate phones across different invitations. Returning an unavailable invitation after reuse is simpler than maintaining replay receipts and cannot reset a previously created account's password.

Use a bounded in memory request limiter and a fixed password hashing capacity for this single process application. A shared store would survive process restarts and coordinate replicas, but introduces infrastructure that the current deployment does not need. Record those limits rather than claiming distributed protection.

Treat country alignment as fixture and policy work. Existing phone numbers and money cannot be converted safely by replacing a prefix or relabelling a currency. The additive migration preserves stored accounts; the explicitly run demo seed supplies new synthetic Thai records. A fixed `Asia/Bangkok` constant retains D15's original purpose of consistent shop day boundaries.

- [ ] Exceed 20 requests per 60 seconds, test the 10,000 key cap with an injected clock, and occupy both hashing slots. Confirm 429 and usable `Retry-After`, without database or hashing work after rejection. Covers **AC-8**.

Confirm a UTC time crossing midnight in Bangkok is displayed on the correct shop date. Covers **AC-10**, **AC-11**.

- [ ] Run `bun run test`, `bun run typecheck`, `bun run lint`, and `bun run format:check`; record exit codes and any blockers. Covers **AC-11**.

**AC-1** through **AC-11** are covered above. Record the commands, response status and safe fields, queries and results, and screenshot paths during `/check verify`. Do not mark a criterion met from code inspection alone.

A0–A2: Browser-first Admin qualification, modular refactor and Integration Store UI gate
# Admin-first browser audit and Integration Store modularization gate
**Baseline (2026-10-27):** `main` `a75e6b5ec436df25a9ac6ba82fc6b36e9e945e1d` (PR #53). This issue is design/research/qualification scope ONLY; **no code restructuring, Production write, deployment or integration activation has been made by this issue**.

## Approval and strict execution order
1. **A0 Human-observable browser walk** — one continuous, browser-driven, role-correct Admin session, starting from login; follow only links/buttons/search/forms visible in the UI. Do not use direct deep links, APIs, database calls, DevTools/JS injection, server-only shortcuts or fixture mutations to *perform this walkthrough*. Preserve video/trace/screenshot/time/commit evidence. Review environment preferred for sample form/file interactions; never pay, send mail, register domains or provision in Production. Test additional role views by normal sign-out/sign-in only.
2. **A1 Safe Admin architecture refactor** — using A0 route/call-site evidence, split feature configs and long components; create redirects only for clearly deprecated navigation after approval; remove legacy files **only after** dependency analysis + tests + verified browser parity. No API/schema/secret/payment authority changes.
3. **A2 Integration Store UI + vendor logo sourcing** — match Octalve Booking searchable provider cards and filters, use accessible per-provider side sheet. Catalogue state vs connection state separated; real vendor-specific form inputs remain unavailable until secure backend B is qualified. Logos: official source/brand rules, locally bundled verified sanitized assets, license/attribution ledger, fallback icon.
4. **B–H** credential/authority, DirectAdmin+WHM, OPanel dual-panel, registrar/DNS, mail/SSL, VPS/dedicated/data-centre and operational certification, each separate reviewed gates.

## Verified code baseline (source, not browser)
- 84 Admin page entry points, 14 Settings sections; 134 total routes x 6 viewports = 804 planned browser cases; `frontend/scripts/browser-parity-qualification.cjs` expressly says browser evidence **PENDING**.
- `frontend/src/app/admin/layout.tsx` uses `RoleGuard allowed={["admin"]}`; JS role guard does **not** replace Django enforcement.
- Current `/admin/servers/new` renders generic `AdminResourceEditorView`, with generic provider `base_url/username/api_key/secret/status` fields in `features/admin/data/admin-editor-config.ts`.
- `AdminResourceEditorView.tsx` ~335 lines; `CatalogAuthorityWorkbench.tsx` ~256 lines /22KB; `admin-workspace-config.ts` ~292 lines. They combine concerns and should be split by domain while preserving semantics.
- Main installed Django provider app: `backend/providers/` (`providers.apps.ProvidersConfig`). There is also `backend/apps/providers/` with a separate adapter registry; **audit imports before deleting or consolidating**. Existing `payments`, `domains`, `catalog`, `provisioning`, and independent `octalve-opanel` retain business authority.
- `octalve-booking` `components/booking/WorkspaceViews.tsx` provides searchable integration grid/card filters; its integration POST endpoint is presently disabled and **not** reusable as a live credential service.
- OPanel vendor read-back supports guarded DirectAdmin/WHM lookup; unrestricted technical writes and dual-panel management are not yet qualified.

## A0: one continuous click-path protocol (strictly no deep-link jumps)
- Open public Console address > use visible Log in > authenticate by form > reach Admin Overview; record visible version/URL + role.
- Navigate all **visible Admin sidebar categories** in order: Command (Overview, Customers, Staff); Commerce (Category, Products, Plans, Orders, Invoices, Transactions); Infrastructure (Services, Domains, Gateways, Providers, Provisioning); Operations (Support, Knowledge Base, Rewards, Reports, Audit Logs, Route Audit, Settings).
- For each destination, use on-page search, filter, sort and pagination if visibly offered; open a record by clicking its row, use visible Back/breadcrumb to return; note broken links, loading states, unqualified Save actions, spacing, accessibility, real/placeholder data, and role errors. Never fabricate fixture record IDs.
- In Settings, open all 14 sections **by selecting cards** from hub, navigate actual related links and return through UI. Verify Providers opens real hosting records, Gateways separate payment records, domain records separate from registrar, Catalogue separate retail pricing. Record ambiguous duplicated destinations.
- In Providers, click Add provider (do not submit real credentials); observe dropdown options and how model/status is presented; test blank/invalid *local* form validation only in isolated Review, no server mutations. For any available logo upload in Review, select a harmless local sample through the file picker, only if feature is visibly offered; otherwise mark not available.
- Follow user-accessible navigation to invoice designer, catalogue workbench, support and approval workflows. Never mark a paid invoice, purchase domain, send email, or execute remote provisioning.
- Test responsive UI and focus/keyboard Escape/Tab/Shift+Tab on a separate browser-led pass while keeping the same navigational flow; test mobile width via browser viewport rather than altering application code.
- Finish via visible Logout. Other roles: repeat by ordinary login with authorized test accounts in isolated Review only. **No skip to /admin/... paths via URL bar except the initial public site/login address.**
- Collect evidence: ordered click ledger, browser screenshots/trace, failing action, URL after click, reproducibility, release SHA, environment, account role, viewport. Tests based solely on source inspection cannot pass A0.

## Proposed route ownership (preserve stable URLs until A0 passes)
- `/admin` remains dashboard.
- `/admin/settings` remains Settings; existing `/admin/settings/providers` becomes discovery link to **Integrations** without new independent secrets.
- `/admin/servers` remains legacy provider record route until integration migration qualifies; never blindly remove existing records or endpoints.
- Proposed `/admin/integrations` as store (after A0/A1); `/admin/integrations/connections` as installed/authorized connections. Sheets are URL-addressable only if a real user can reach through store cards; guard deep-route reload.
- `/admin/gateways` preserves payment/financial authority; `/admin/catalog/workbench` preserves retail pricing; OPanel remains independent repo.

## Proposed modular frontend tree (A1/A2 target, NOT yet created)
```
frontend/src/app/admin/                # thin route entry points, auth layout
frontend/src/features/admin/
  overview/
  customers/
  staff/
  commerce/{catalog,orders,invoices,transactions,billing}/
  infrastructure/{services,domains,provisioning}/
  integrations/
    catalog/{manifests,categories,search}/
    connections/{list,details,status}/
    sheets/{IntegrationSheet,Requirements,Configuration,Verification}/
    adapters/{hosting,registrars,dns,ssl,mail,payments,cloud,vps}/
    assets/{sources,usage-ledger}/
    shared/{types,components,validation}/
  operations/{support,knowledge,reports,audit}/
  settings/
  shared/{components,hooks,types,api}/
```
Keep feature modules cohesive and typically <=200–250 lines, with thin route adapters. Do not split a 30-line cohesive component solely to inflate file count. Preserve existing shared `features/shell` and design-system; do not copy shell, pricing, payments, or entitlement logic. Adapter manifests are **server-authored/versioned**; TS UI may only render approved fields, never define outbound authority.

## Detailed refactor acceptance gates
- Before changes: capture all existing link destinations, API operations, permissions and baseline CI. Classify duplicate pages as redirect / reuse / retained / safe to retire; no unverified deletion.
- After each narrowly scoped PR: exact SHA TypeScript/Next build, Django/security, source-to-route and owner scopes, financial write guard, provider adapter security and browser visual parity on representative workflows.
- A1 no business write behaviour changes; same API paths, same customer session, same invoice/payment rules, same provider records, OPanel SSO unchanged; no new migrations.
- Store logo sourcing: prefer official vendor press/brand-kit SVG/PNG, original aspect/color, no implied partnership; security-sanitize SVG or use approved raster, local immutable filenames, record brand usage restrictions and documentation URLs.
- A2 side sheet: desktop right panel and mobile full-screen sheet, focus trap, accessible name, Escape close, background inert, close-button, return focus, unsaved-change confirmation, responsive scroll. Vendor-level availability distinct from specific connection state.
- B secrets only after backend has deny-by-default role checks, isolated encryption/rotation, SSRF protection and immutable audit. Store UI cannot make an adapter executable.
- Do **not** use screenshots, demos or signed manifests alone as evidence of successful authenticated browser interaction; signoff must attest real browser behavior.
- Production deploy and alias health remain separate from green GitHub CI; Vercel build-rate limit currently unresolved.

## Reference standards
- Next.js App Router intercepting/parallel routes: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/intercepting-routes
- W3C dialog modal keyboard/focus: https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/dialog-modal/
- Playwright authenticated browser use and sensitive cookies: https://playwright.dev/docs/auth
- OWASP Web Security Testing Guide: https://owasp.org/projects/web-security-testing-guide
- OWASP Secrets Management: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html
- Vendor logos: https://www.directadmin.com/extras-logos.php ; https://www.cpanel.net/company/cpanel-brand-guide/

## Summary
`README.md` gives two different counts for the same thing (88 and 83 specialized agents), and none matches the files. Its structure tree also shows folders at the repo root that live under `.hanzo/agents/`.

## Evidence
Checked at `6ab6811`.

- `ls .hanzo/agents/definitions | grep -v '^README' | wc -l` prints `108`. The role-based table at `README.md:326-366` lists 16 of them, which leaves 92, not 88 or 83.
- "42 development tools": `README.md:49`, `:62`, `:278`, `:765`. `ls .hanzo/agents/tools | wc -l` prints `43`.
- "15 workflows" is right: `ls .hanzo/agents/workflows | wc -l` prints `15`.
- The tree at `README.md:266-281` draws `agents/`, `workflows/` and `tools/` at the root; `ls agents workflows tools` finds none of them.

## What to do
Pick one counting rule and write it down in the README (for example: specialized = files in `.hanzo/agents/definitions/` that are not in the role-based table). Recount, then make every count in the file agree with it and with `ls`. Redraw the tree with the real `.hanzo/agents/` layout.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `grep -n -E '\b(83|88|92|108)\b.*agents' README.md` shows one number for specialized agents, the same everywhere.
- [ ] The tools and workflows counts equal `ls .hanzo/agents/tools | wc -l` and `ls .hanzo/agents/workflows | wc -l`.
- [ ] The tree lists paths that exist (`.hanzo/agents/definitions`, `.hanzo/agents/workflows`, `.hanzo/agents/tools`).
- [ ] The counting rule appears once in the README and the pull request shows the commands used to recount.

source_text:
> Im not labelling any job stupid, im simply saying they are simple and there is no justification to pay hundreds of dollars a week for anything that 
> Im not labelling any job stupid, im simply saying they are simple and there is no justification to pay hundreds of dollars a week for anything that AI may help. Neither was I; I was saying that the US spending 9% of its own GDP looks a bit silly if that AI is only used within the USA's own economy. > No argument about calculators, but most job wouldnt pay hundreds of dollars a week for the utility of a calculator. Today vs. before the tech existed? Today: That's because calculators cost single-digit dollars/pounds/euros. Yet if you took a calculator back in time a century, it's not inconceivable that businesses  whose job involves lots of arithmetic  would value it at 10-15% of average wages, given the labour it would save. However, as you may have noticed, a calculator doesn't do every job. I see the same applying to AI, at least for now: for jobs where it's useful, it's worth 10-15% of wages. This isn't all jobs. Regardless of if it was all jobs or not, the tech gets cheaper, and just as nobody can charge more than a single digit $£€ for a basic 4-function calculator, nobody will be able to charge 10-15% of average wages for 2026 AI even a year from now let alone a century. > Your friend might be good with their hands, but they are not going to have the equipment for most jobs. WHen you buy the services of a plumber or any other tradesperson you are not only buying their skills, you are also leveraging their equipment. I don't mean "your friend". I mean pretend you're founding a new house repair firm: do you hire expert plumbers, or do you hire (presumably in a few years because neither the AI nor the AR is good enough today) random people willing to follow instructions from their AR glasses? You've bought all the equipment etc. the same in both cases. Who do you hire? And when everyone does that, do you as a customer prefer to hire the cheap company whose staff are as described, or the traditional firm that's 3x the price? Before you scoff:  this kind of thing has happened repeatedly with previous technologies . The main difference with the current architecture of modern AI is how general purpose it is, not that this is new. Previous architectures of AI were more like a normal technology, making one thing obsolete at a time, like  manually reading letters in a post sorting office , but just that and nothing else. High-skill roles get some automation, that turns them into low-skill roles. Suddenly, their bosses don't need to spend so much on wages to get the tasks done.  That's  the point with my cashier example. Someone working as a cashier in 1876 needed to be good at mental arithmetic, if I showed them a pocket calculator they might be impressed but in this context I'd expect them to be insulted: why would they need that for their job? Then the mechanical one was invented (to avoid embezzlement), and suddenly their bosses didn't need to hire people with that skill.

source_text:
COMPUTE-MFG-001C: PCB fabrication, assembly, rework, and test capability profile
Parent: [COMPUTE-MFG-001 #5796](https://github.com/Luminous-Dynamics/symthaea/issues/5796). Compose [MFG-PROC-000 #5686](https://github.com/Luminous-Dynamics/symthaea/issues/5686), [MFG-PROC-001 #5688](https://github.com/Luminous-Dynamics/symthaea/issues/5688), [HMI-MFG-001B #5799](https://github.com/Luminous-Dynamics/symthaea/issues/5799), [SEMI-ROADMAP-001 #5867](https://github.com/Luminous-Dynamics/symthaea/issues/5867), existing fabrication authority and evidence/metrology owners, plus [AtomFab PCB productive-closure roadmap PR #8222](https://github.com/Luminous-Dynamics/symthaea/pull/8222).

## Purpose

Freeze the first executable, evidence-bounded benchmark for designing, routing, fabricating or sourcing, assembling, inspecting, repairing, and testing a small low-voltage PCB.

This is the PCB-specific implementation slice of the existing computer/electronics closure program. It does not create a parallel process ontology, BOM authority, inspection ledger, capability-closure engine, or machine-control path.

## Core distinctions

~~~text
PCB design exists != design passes declared DRC/DFM
Gerber/drill export exists != bare board has been fabricated
bare board passes inspection != assembly is functional
local assembly != local bare-board production
local bare-board production != local IC/passive/connector manufacture
chip RTL/design != fabricated, packaged, tested silicon
~~~

## First article profile

Use a repairable low-voltage 2-layer sensor/controller board or wired macropad, selected and frozen after a design-for-manufacture review. Keep the first article outside mains voltage, high-energy power conversion, and safety-critical control.

Track independently: native design and library dependencies; electrical netlist; BOM / substitutes; manufacturing output bundle; bare-board route; assembly recipe; as-built identity; firmware identity; required inspection and electrical/functional test evidence; repair/rework history.

## Route profiles to compare

- **P0: outsourced bare board + local assembly/test.** Supplier service and lot are explicit external dependencies.
- **P1: local isolation milling/drilling + local assembly/test.** Admissible only for feature requirements actually supported by the exact machine/material/tool/fixture profile; do not assume plated-through vias, industrial solder mask/finish, multilayer, impedance control, or high-density capability.
- **P2: image/etch prototype route.** Representation only unless separately reviewed site/process safety and waste-management profiles are present; this issue gives no chemical recipe or operating setpoint.
- **P3: conventional multilayer route.** Keep as an external qualified supplier profile initially; model internal lamination, drilling, desmear/plating, mask/finish, and electrical-test capability only as separate future qualification stages.

## Synthetic corpus

Freeze at least 16 small known-answer cases before implementing route selection. Include positive controls and negative controls for:

1. valid P0 route with supplier capability evidence and complete output bundle;
2. valid simple P1 route with no plated vias;
3. P1 requested for plated-through vias;
4. P1 requested for multilayer stack-up;
5. route's minimum trace/space capability unknown;
6. missing or stale DRC/DFM evidence;
7. missing or revision-mismatched drill output;
8. required solder mask or surface finish unavailable in selected route;
9. unapproved component substitution changes a protected BOM requirement;
10. missing required bare-board inspection;
11. stale/missing calibration for a measurement used for acceptance;
12. missing assembly/placement artifact;
13. solder/placement inspection incomplete for the product profile;
14. functional tests use wrong firmware or board revision;
15. missing lot/as-built provenance;
16. synthetic or supplier-declared results incorrectly promoted as independent physical qualification.

The independent oracle must derive dispositions from profile/case relationships, not echo expected output fields. Include duplicate IDs, wrong schema, altered case count, mismatched digests and missing negative controls as corpus-integrity attacks.

## Acceptance and metrics

- 100% agreement with independently derived known-answer dispositions.
- 100% rejection of the registered invalid routes; all unresolved prerequisites return **incomplete** or **reject**, never silent pass.
- Process feasibility, board quality, assembly quality, functional results, cost, lead time, resource impact, repairability and import dependence stay as separate outputs; no scalar score can override a hard gate.
- Every route and receipt binds exact design revision, netlist/BOM, route/capability profile, schema/corpus digest, tool versions and Git HEAD.
- Input order does not change canonical identity; a material, netlist, recipe, profile or protected-datum change changes the appropriate subject identity.
- Physical targets for trace/space, drill accuracy, yield and reliability are defined from the actual article/product class and measured with suitable instruments; do not infer them from commanded step size or simulation.
- Cost per accepted board includes labour, setup, consumables, tool wear, depreciation, utilities, inspection, scrap, rework and external supplier charges; disclose sample size and uncertainty.

## Implementation sequence

1. Freeze the schema / fixture contract and independent oracle.
2. Add deterministic Rust validation and a reproducible receipt; run locally before relying on hosted CI.
3. Add a KiCad CLI export / package-inventory adapter behind the existing process contract; never execute machine outputs from untrusted or unvalidated design input.
4. Connect to the existing fabrication gateway only for already-qualified, explicitly authorized process profiles.
5. Add as-built, netlist, inspection, functional-test and repair evidence composition.
6. Extend to SMT automation / OpenPnP only after the first article and its manual baseline are reproducible.

## Non-goals

No machine actuation or new execution authority; no hazardous process recipes; no claim of multilayer production qualification; no claim of locally fabricated semiconductors; no claim that passing synthetic cases establishes physical yields or reliability.

How to Choose Cables and Switchgear for Solar and Wind Projects in India
A solar farm or wind plant is only as dependable as the electrical network behind it. Panels and turbines generate the power, but cables, terminations and switchgear carry, protect and control it for 20–25 years. Bharat Trading Corporation (BTC), a Pune-based supplier of wires, cables and switchgear, explains how to choose these components. For the full walkthrough, read our[ Cable and Switchgear Selection Guide for Renewable Energy (Solar/Wind) Installations](https://btc.net.in/cable-and-switchgear-selection-guide-for-renewable-energy-solar-wind-installations/).
Why Component Selection Matters
Renewable sites face sun, heat, rain, dust and vibration every day. Weak insulation or poorly matched switchgear leads to voltage loss, insulation failure and unplanned shutdowns. Specifying correctly at the start means fewer maintenance visits and a better-protected investment. BTC’s[ renewable energy industry page](https://btc.net.in/renewable-energy-industry/) shows how this applies across solar, wind, hydro and hybrid plants.
Follow the Power: Where Each Component Fits
DC collection: Solar DC cables connect panels to combiner boxes and inverters.
Conversion: Inverters or turbine controllers convert DC to AC.
AC distribution: Armoured or heavy-duty power cables feed switchgear, breakers, control panels and transformers.
Monitoring: Control and instrumentation cables support SCADA and automation.
Export or storage: Well-terminated wiring carries energy to the grid or battery systems.
Choosing the Right Cables
Solar DC cables (single and twin core): Built for high DC voltage, UV exposure and outdoor weather. See BTC’s[ solar cable](https://btc.net.in/product/solar-cable-is-17293/).
Armoured and unarmoured power cables: Used for AC distribution and transformer connections. Armoured types add protection for underground or exposed runs.
Control and instrumentation cables: Keep monitoring and plant automation accurate.
Copper vs aluminium: Copper gives higher conductivity and compact sizing. Aluminium is lighter and more economical for long runs across large solar farms.
FRLS vs LSZH: FRLS limits flame spread and smoke. LSZH releases minimal smoke and no halogen gases, which suits enclosed plant rooms.
Explore the full range of[ wires and cables](https://btc.net.in/product-category/wires-and-cables/), including[ RR Kabel](https://btc.net.in/rr-kable-supplier/) and[ Dynamic Cable](https://btc.net.in/dynamic-cable-supplier/).
Terminations and Protective Accessories
A cable is only as reliable as its connection. BTC supplies[ cable lugs and glands](https://btc.net.in/product-category/lugs-gland/) for secure, vibration-resistant terminations, heat shrink sleeves for weatherproof sealing, and[ cable ducts](https://btc.net.in/product-category/cable-ducts/) and[ cable ties](https://btc.net.in/product-category/cable-tie/) for organised, maintainable wiring.
Switchgear for Renewable Installations
Once AC power leaves the inverter or turbine controller, switchgear controls, protects and isolates circuits. This lets operators de-energise one section for maintenance without shutting down the whole plant. BTC supplies[ switchgear](https://btc.net.in/product-category/switchgear/) through Schneider Electric, so you can[ view our Schneider Electric supplier page](https://btc.net.in/schneider-electric-supplier/). Match it to site conditions such as outdoor exposure, temperature swings, dust and moisture. Sourcing cables and switchgear together helps teams plan distribution, protection and control as one coordinated system.
Challenges to Plan For
Plan for UV and weather exposure, 600V–1500V DC stress in solar systems, turbine vibration, moisture in hydro plants, corrosion near coastal sites, and voltage drop over long runs.
Get the Right Components from One Supplier
BTC brings together solar DC cables, power and control cabling, terminations and Schneider Electric switchgear. Browse our wires and cables supplier and[ switchgear supplier](https://btc.net.in/switchgear-supplier/) pages, or[ contact BTC](https://btc.net.in/contact-us/) for help with your project.
About Us
Bharat Trading Corporation (BTC) is a supplier of electrical and industrial products, offering a wide range of wires, cables, switchgear, terminal blocks, cable ducts, sleeves, cable ties, LED and lighting products, tools, panel accessories, motors, lugs and glands, and other electrical components. BTC works with products and brands serving industries such as construction, automation, power transmission, food and beverage, OEMs, renewable energy, railways, data and communication, and more. With a broad product portfolio, BTC aims to provide reliable electrical and industrial solutions for different business requirements.
Contact Us
For product enquiries, electrical goods and accessories requirements, or business enquiries, you can contact Bharat Trading Corporation (BTC).

Review: ECON-F13-420-A1
### Contribution handle

ECON-F13-420-A1

### Finding

Supports the claim

### What you checked

Two-supplier quadratic shortage model; arbitrary baseline share and policy-dependent worst disruption dependence

Contribution `con_d99f600dafb5417391047bba1348d67c`; revision `rev_a64bf3e2db4e450caf338b5c2ee9df35`; source commit `bd5218964aa5efa77ac062e3600b8cfe70df528c`.

### Evidence

# A complete robust sourcing solution for an interior baseline

The source correctly notes that an interior baseline changes which dependence endpoint is worst, so its closed-form solution for x⁰=0 cannot simply be reused. The general interior-baseline problem is still exactly solvable. It is a concave three-piece objective, not an unconstrained search over disruption laws and policies.

Retain all primitives of the two-supplier model, including feasible joint failure probabilities q∈[q_−,q_+]. Fix any baseline x₀∈[0,1] and define

a(q)=p₁+p₂−2q≥0,
d(q)=2L(p₂−q)−Δc.

Expanding the same-law welfare difference gives

G_q(x)=d(q)(x−x₀)−La(q)(x²−x₀²).

Its coefficient on q is −2L[x(1−x)−x₀(1−x₀)]. Let l=min{x₀,1−x₀} and u=max{x₀,1−x₀}. The concave parabola x(1−x) is at least its baseline value exactly on [l,u]. Consequently the robust improvement is

G(x)=G_{q_+}(x) for l≤x≤u,
G(x)=G_{q_−}(x) for 0≤x≤l or u≤x≤1.

At l and u the two endpoint values agree, so there is no ambiguity in this formula. It also covers x₀=0 or1, when the central interval is the entire domain and the source's upper-endpoint dependence result is recovered.

Each G_q is a concave quadratic. More generally G=inf_q G_q is concave: for x,y and θ∈[0,1], every G_q(θx+(1−θ)y) is at least θG_q(x)+(1−θ)G_q(y), which is at least θinf_r G_r(x)+(1−θ)inf_r G_r(y). Taking the infimum over q preserves that lower bound. Thus the endpoint switching does not introduce a nonconcave objective.

An explicit finite solution follows. On each of the three closed intervals [0,l], [l,u], [u,1], use its assigned q endpoint. If a(q)>0, the quadratic maximizer on an interval [r,s] is

x_[r,s](q)=min{s,max{r,d(q)/(2La(q))}}.

Evaluate G at those at most three candidates and select the largest value. If a(q)=0, the objective on that interval is linear: choose its right endpoint when d(q)>0, its left endpoint when d(q)<0, and any point when d(q)=0. Degenerate intervals produce repeated candidates and cause no problem. Every interval maximum is attained, so choosing the best candidate proves global attainment and optimality.

There is also a simple uniqueness criterion. If a(q_+)>0, then a(q)≥a(q_+) for every admissible q. The functions G_q(x)+La(q_+)x² are all concave, and so is their infimum. Hence G is strongly concave with quadratic curvature at least 2La(q_+), and its maximizer is unique. If a(q_+)=0, uniqueness may fail and should not be claimed automatically. This includes identical marginal failures with perfectly common failure permitted.

The baseline itself satisfies G(x₀)=0. The optimized robust gain is therefore nonnegative under this feasible-policy menu, even though a particular alternative may have a negative guarantee. The chosen adverse endpoint can differ across policies and is always applied to policy and baseline under the same law; separate minimization of their welfare levels would answer another question.

This completes the exact optimization for arbitrary baselines in the declared divisible two-supplier subclass. It does not identify failure dependence, add inventories or substitution, or deliver a general-equilibrium reshoring ranking. No external result is needed for the formula or proof.

source_text:
[tooling] the triage board never promotes land-candidates to triage:pareto, so 391 scored PRs are unprotected and due for the sweep
`CONTRIBUTING.md` and `tools/queue_sweeper.py` both state that the daily triage board promotes land-candidates to `triage:pareto`, which is what keeps them out of the 5-day sweep. No code path does that. The promotion is documented but never executed.

## What the docs promise

`CONTRIBUTING.md:48-50`:

> Rebased reopens re-enter triage as fresh arrivals, and the daily board promotes land-candidates `triage:pareto` automatically.

`tools/queue_sweeper.py:42`, in the close-comment every swept PR receives:

> the daily triage board promotes land-candidates to `triage:pareto` (protected) automatically.

## What the code does

Three separate facts, each verifiable on `1f0ff97`:

**1. `classify()` does compute the right label.** `tools/triage_bot.py:323-325`:

```python
elif s >= 6:
    it["bucket"] = "LAND-CANDIDATE"
    lab.append("triage:pareto")
```

So the intent exists and the scoring is correct.

**2. But only `cmd_labels` writes it,** and `cmd_labels` is reachable solely through `triage_bot.py labels --apply`. Grepping every workflow:

```
$ grep -rln 'labels --apply' .github/workflows/
(no output)
```

Nothing invokes it. `triage-board.yml` runs `board --post` and `approve --max 60`; `shepherd-board.yml` runs `scan`, `board --post --from-scan`, and `shepherd.py sync-labels`.

**3. `sync-labels` is not a substitute.** `tools/shepherd.py:154-156`:

```python
mapping = {"LAND-CANDIDATE": "bot:land-candidate",
           "CONFLICTS": "bot:conflict",
           "STALE-BASE": "bot:stale-base"}
```

`LAND-CANDIDATE` maps to `bot:land-candidate`, never to `triage:pareto`. `triage:pareto` does not appear anywhere in `shepherd.py`. And `bot:land-candidate` is not in `PROTECTED_LABELS` (`queue_sweeper.py:30`), which is exactly `{triage:wildcard-hold, triage:pareto, triage:keep}`.

## The consequence, measured

```
open PRs with bot:land-candidate                 428
  ... of which also have triage:pareto            37
  ... therefore scored land-candidate, unprotected 391
```

Those 391 have cleared the scoring bar the project itself defines for "worth landing" and still carry no protection from the sweep. They survive only while they stay under `SWEEPER_MIN_AGE_DAYS`, which means the auto-promotion failure is invisible for the first five days and then removes exactly the PRs the board had ranked highest.

`#2202` (mine, so treat it as a self-interested data point rather than a neutral one) is one of the 391: score 9/9, bucket `LAND-CANDIDATE`, label `bot:land-candidate`, no `triage:pareto`, created `2026-10-29T10:06:38Z`, sweep due `2026-11-04 05:15 UTC`.

## Why it has not surfaced yet

The doctrine change that introduced the sweep landed `2026-10-24` (`2149be1`, `83f6bda`). The first sweep that can act on a post-doctrine PR runs five days later. `2026-10-29` is day five, so the gap has had almost no window in which to destroy anything visible, and the queue it is about to bite is 391 PRs deep.

The `2026-10-29 05:10` `triage-board` run also failed with `403 API rate limit exceeded for installation` while paginating `/pulls?page=2`, aborting before `sync-labels` could run at all. That is a separate, secondary problem (the board needs a token budget headroom fix), but it means even the `bot:*` sync did not complete today.

## Fix shape

Whichever of these the maintainer prefers, the point is that the docs and the code must agree:

- **Cheapest:** add `labels --apply --from-scan` to `triage-board.yml` after the scan, before the sweep window. One step, uses the scan that already ran.
- **Or** map `LAND-CANDIDATE` to `triage:pareto` inside `sync-labels` and widen `PROTECTED_LABELS`. This keeps one label-writing path but changes what `bot:land-candidate` means, so the two labels would need distinguishing.
- **Or** amend the two documents to say the promotion is manual. That is the honest option if automation is deliberately not wanted here, but then the sweep is closing land-candidates and the copy should say so plainly instead of promising a promotion that never fires.

I do not have write access to `automation/` or the workflows, so this is a report, not a patch.

## Anything else

**AI disclosure.** Prepared by an AI agent, as permitted by `BOUNTY.md`. Every claim above was produced by running the commands shown against `1f0ff97`; the two label counts come from the GitHub search API, and the file/line references were read from the tree rather than inferred.

source_text:
Yarn shop - customisable yarn kit with real-time inventory syncing
I’ve looked all through the community topics many times, and there are several threads existing already for this question.  But so far, I haven’t found an answer to this problem, nor have I found an app that can do exactly what I want.  Some apps can do part of it, but none work completely.  So here is the problem: 
 I own a yarn shop (knitting and crochet).  As well as the yarn itself, I also offer a range of kits of sweaters that use yarns that I sell, so that customers can buy the yarn and pattern in one easy go.  At the moment the only way I can do this is to ask them to check the stock levels for their size and then specify the colours they want in the comments box before checking out.  Then I have to manually adjust the stock.  It’s really not ideal, as too often customers just don’t check and ask for colours that are out of stock, or they just don’t specify anything at all as they don’t understand what to do.  Also it relies on me adjusting stock quickly so that no-one else then tries to buy yarn that is already spoken for.  I waste a lot of time emailing customers to clarify. 
 So for example:  a sweater may require 2 different colours and be available in 8 different sizes, each of which requires a different amount of yarn per colour.  The yarn used for the sweater may be available in 25 different colours.  Customers should be able to choose their own colour combination and not be restricted to certain colours only. 
 So on the kit product page, they would first choose their size - this would determine how many balls of wool they need for each colour. 
 Then they would choose the main colour from a dropdown/colour swatch panel. 
 Then they would choose the secondary colour from a second dropdown/colour swatch panel. 
 When they choose their colours, this should somehow sync with the stock on the actual yarn product to make sure that they can’t choose a colour that doesn’t have enough stock for their size, and also to adjust the stock on the yarn product so that I don’t have to do it manually.  This is an example (on a Shopify store) to show what I mean: 
 
   
       

       Önling INT 
   

   
       

  Dagfrid Sweater, No 3 knitting kit  

   Knitting kit for Dagfrid Sweater – an Icelandic sweater featuring a beautiful three-dimensional pattern. Knitted in organic, heavy merino wool Önling No 3 


   

   
    
    
   

    
 

 It seems that comments on these threads indicate that there are a lot of other Shopify merchants out there with yarn shops who need the exact same thing, so I’m surprised that no expert so far has tried to create an app and market it as I’m sure there would be plenty of interest in it. 
 I’d be interested in hearing from any other yarn shop owners who have found a solution (either via an existing app or with a custom app) or from any app developer who has made apps that can do this.

Firstly, take everything that I say with a grain of salt. I can only reply on to the things that you've told here and give advice from it but I don't 
Firstly, take everything that I say with a grain of salt. I can only reply on to the things that you've told here and give advice from it but I don't know the full situation. Read the advice and apply it as you wish. > I have been staying up late, sleeping in, skipping chores, neglecting my relationships, eating too much food, neglecting hygiene, and generally just being a bum. Happens with me. Something which helps me is figuring out why I sleep late. For me, it was a constant cycle of trying to do something today's night to cope up with waking up late or not doing something today. Realize that productivity = hours put in * focus. I found myself constantly procastinating (hours go down) and when doing tasks (with less focus) And if you continue this cycle, then the cycle continues. Over a long term, it is better for you to sleep today no matter how the day went early and then wake up early. It has been scientifically shown to improve your mental health and even from the logical standpoint of productivity, it will be better to sleep early today than not. Your time is constant, when you sleep late you are borrowing time from tomorrow's productivity and this borrowing cycle will continue and you will feel as if you are short on time but you have ample amount of time provided you break the cycle. Don't Neglect your relationships: Here's a comment[0] that I recently wrote about it. TLDR: try to appreciate them back and don't take them for granted. Appreciate them a lot. There is some logic that I have found in that struggle is finite and constant and you can either take it in small doses today rather than an instant hit later. This also applies to doing chores Regarding cleanliness: My room is a mess but the logic which can help is that I have found myself losing so so many time because I lost my keys or just lost something and then it has an insane amount of stress/time loss and struggle. I had forgotten (twice) that I had already taken my clothes back from laundry because of how messy my room is and I had to manually count all clothes I have (twice). The amount of struggle in keeping your room clean is better than keeping it not clean. Also, even speaking out of logical arguments, right now if I understand you, you want to be the guy who does keep his room clean, who does sleep early and who does appreciate relationships. You don't want the immediate benefits of it as much as you want it to help be part of your identity and boost its self-confidence. You want to be the guy as you want to do something, anything. > My main reason has been that I am afraid of interviewing and that my skills are not up to par. Happens with me as well but again the struggle is constant if not larger. You can either do interviews right now and fail them (which is okay, literally everyone fails) and failure teaches more than success. You learn from it, you improve and your fear can be taken less. Fear is because of the fact that you aren't approaching it, not that you aren't approaching it because of fear. In some sense, its a chicken and egg problem and the only way to break out of it is to not give the fear enough importance to make you change decisions but rather act on it and pass through its struggle and win through it. Do the interviews right now,don't postpone/procastinate it. Try to give as much as possible and not expect anything in return. because if so, then what is it to fear? Worst case: you don't get the job, best case: you do. Well if you don't interview, its already the worst case plus you are giving fear its weight. If you notice, I am saying the same thing over and over again applying more weight to it each time but I think that this overarching philosophy does help me sometimes to be more comfortable with struggling to then be a better person because I want to be a better person and I am gonna struggle. Might as well struggle (less) and then be a person I am proud of being. Once again, I doubt that the thing stopping you is knowledge. I have tried to give knowledge but in today's world, it's not because you lack some knowledge that is causing you this but rather the lack of actions. One action can speak more and form your identity better than reading books and speaking all you want. Your brain asks you: Talk is cheap, show me the actions.
